name: English
title: Basic Knowledge Test, Canton of Zurich

q001.question: Switzerland is neutral. What does that mean?

options.a: It does not sign any international treaties.
options.b: It only concludes treaties with states that are not involved in wars.
options.c: It does not get involved in armed conflicts between other states.
options.d: It wants to be economically independent as a transit country.

q001.why: Neutrality means: Switzerland does not take part in wars between other states and does not support any warring party militarily.

distractors.a: Switzerland signs a great many international treaties and is a member of the UN.
distractors.b: Neutrality does not forbid treaties; Switzerland also has trade relations with states that are at war.
distractors.d: Neutrality is a rule for wars, not an economic goal as a transit country.

q002.question: What is a cross-border commuter (Grenzgänger)?

options.a: a person who works in Switzerland and lives abroad
options.b: a person who does not live and work in the same canton
options.c: Swiss goods that are exported abroad
options.d: Swiss goods that are imported into Switzerland from abroad

q002.why: A cross-border commuter lives abroad and crosses the border to work in Switzerland. After work, she returns home again.

distractors.b: A person who works in another canton is a commuter. They do not cross a national border.
distractors.c: Cross-border commuters are people, not goods. Goods that are sent abroad are called exports.

q003.question: Confoederatio Helvetica ...

options.a: is the name of a Swiss chocolate.
options.b: is the Latin name for the Swiss Confederation.
options.c: is the name of Switzerland's first parliament.
options.d: is a parliamentary group in Parliament.

q003.why: «Confoederatio» is Latin for «confederation», and the Helvetii once lived in the area of Switzerland. So the name means Swiss Confederation in Latin.

distractors.c: The first Federal Parliament of 1848 was called the Federal Assembly, not Confoederatio Helvetica.
distractors.d: Parliamentary groups are groups of members of Parliament from one party; none of them has this name.

q004.question: Which of these is a department of the Federal Administration?

options.c: Department of Schools and Continuing Education

q004.why: The Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP) is one of the seven departments. Among other things, it is responsible for migration, naturalisation and internal security.

distractors.c: Schools are a matter for the cantons. At federal level, education and research belong to the department EAER (WBF).
distractors.b: Environment and climate belong to DETEC (UVEK). There is no department with this name.
distractors.a: There is no separate food department. Agriculture belongs to the EAER (WBF).

q005.question: The members of the Federal Council are bound by the principle of collegiality. What does that mean?

options.a: The members of the Federal Council must know each other well.
options.b: Each Federal Councillor represents their own political opinions.
options.c: All members must represent the decisions of the Federal Council in the same way in public.
options.d: The Federal Council makes decisions by vote.

q005.why: The Federal Council makes decisions as a body. After that, all seven members represent the decision in the same way in public, even if they personally think differently.

distractors.b: Within the body, the members may say what they think. In public, however, they must represent the joint decision.
distractors.d: The Federal Council does sometimes vote. But the principle of collegiality means that afterwards all members represent the decision together.
distractors.a: Whether the members know each other well does not matter. It is about appearing united in public.

q005.note: In the official German text, option d is missing its verb: «Der Bundesrat Entscheidungen mit Abstimmung.» It probably means «Der Bundesrat fällt Entscheidungen mit Abstimmung.» We show the text as the canton published it.

q006.question: Can voters stop a new law?

options.b: No, only the Federal Council can change laws
options.c: No, only the National Council can change laws

q006.why: With a referendum, the people can vote on a new law before it applies. If the majority says no, the law does not come into force.

distractors.a: An initiative proposes something new for the Constitution. To stop a law passed by Parliament, you need a referendum.
distractors.b: Laws are made by Parliament, not by the Federal Council. And the people can stop them with a referendum.
distractors.c: The National Council does not decide alone; the Council of States must also agree. The people can have the last word.

q007.question: What does the Federal Chancellor of Switzerland do?
q007.why: The Federal Chancellor heads the Federal Chancellery. It is the staff office of the Federal Council and supports it in its work.

distractors.b: Unlike in Germany, the Federal Chancellor does not govern in Switzerland. The government is the Federal Council.
distractors.c: The Federal Council is elected by the United Federal Assembly, not by the Federal Chancellor.
distractors.d: Laws are made by Parliament.

q008.question: In votes, what does «majority of the cantons» (Ständemehr) mean?

options.c: majority of votes by language region of Switzerland
options.d: majority in the preceding opinion polls

q008.why: «Stände» is an old word for the cantons. The majority of the cantons (Ständemehr) is reached when the majority of cantons says yes.

distractors.a: The majority of all votes is called the majority of the people (Volksmehr), not the majority of the cantons (Ständemehr).
distractors.c: Language regions play no role in popular votes. Votes and cantons are counted.

q009.question: What political rights do Swiss citizens living abroad have?

options.a: They may take part in votes and elections when they are visiting Switzerland.
options.b: They lose all political rights in Switzerland.
options.c: They can take part in national votes and elections without having to travel to Switzerland to do so.
options.d: They may not be politically active in any way in their host country.

q009.why: Swiss citizens living abroad keep the right to vote and elect at federal level. The documents arrive by post; in some cantons e-voting is also possible.

distractors.a: A visit to Switzerland is not necessary. You vote from abroad by post.
distractors.b: People who emigrate remain Swiss citizens and keep their political rights.
distractors.d: Switzerland does not forbid them to be active in their host country. That is governed by the law of the host country.

q010.question: Anyone who wants to vote in elections and popular votes in Switzerland …

options.c: must have been born in Switzerland.

q010.why: Political rights at federal level are tied to Swiss citizenship. Without Swiss citizenship, you may not vote in national elections and popular votes.

distractors.c: The place of birth does not matter. People who were born abroad and naturalised later may also vote.
distractors.d: The amount of tax you pay has no influence. Every vote counts the same.

q011.question: What is a political party?

options.a: an association of people from the same town or village
options.b: an association of people with similar political goals
options.c: an association of people with different world views
options.d: an association of National Councillors or Councillors of States in order to reach a majority

q011.why: A party brings together people who think similarly about politics and want to reach their goals together.

distractors.a: The place of residence is not what matters. A party is connected by shared political goals.
distractors.c: A party needs shared goals. People with completely different world views do not form a party.
distractors.d: Most party members are not members of Parliament. Anyone can become a member.

q012.question: Which of these is a task of the Confederation?
q012.why: Switzerland has one common currency, the franc. That is why monetary policy is a matter for the Confederation; the National Bank carries it out.

distractors.c: Policing is mainly a matter for the cantons and municipalities. Each canton has its own cantonal police.
distractors.d: State schools are organised by the cantons and municipalities, not by the Confederation.
distractors.a: Water supply is usually a task of the municipalities.

q013.question: Which of these is a task of the Confederation?
q013.why: Customs checks the border of all of Switzerland. That is why it is a task of the Confederation.

distractors.d: Hospitals are a matter for the cantons, not for the Confederation.
distractors.a: The fire service is organised by the municipalities.

q014.question: Which of these is a fundamental right in Switzerland?
q014.why: Freedom of expression and information is in the Federal Constitution. It is important so that everyone can form their own opinion freely.

distractors.a: Keeping animals is regulated by laws, but it is not a fundamental right in the Constitution.
distractors.c: Television is not a fundamental right. You even pay a fee for radio and television.

q015.question: Which of these is a fundamental right in Switzerland?
q015.why: Freedom of religion and conscience is guaranteed in the Federal Constitution. Every person may freely choose their religion or have none.

distractors.a: Owning weapons is allowed in Switzerland, but strictly regulated. It is not a fundamental right.
distractors.b: Enough housing is a goal of the state, but not a right that you can claim.
distractors.c: Work is a goal of the state, but nobody has a right to a particular job.

q016.question: What obligations do residents of Switzerland have?

options.c: They must have a bank account.
options.d: They must have a driving licence.

q016.why: With taxes, the state pays for schools, roads, the police and much more. Anyone with income or assets must pay taxes.

distractors.b: An apprenticeship is one possible path after school, but it is not an obligation.
distractors.c: A bank account is practical, but it is not required by law.

q017.question: What obligations do residents of Switzerland have?

options.b: They must be a member of a church.
options.c: They must register with the municipality.

q017.why: The municipality must know who lives there, for example for taxes, school and popular votes. That is why you must register after moving there.

distractors.b: Freedom of religion applies. Nobody has to be a member of a church.
distractors.a: Continuing education is voluntary.

q018.question: What obligations do residents of Switzerland have?

options.a: They must be insured against theft.
options.b: They must be insured with a health insurance fund.
options.c: They must have an SBB Half Fare travelcard (Halbtax).

q018.why: Health insurance is compulsory for all people who live in Switzerland. This way every person is insured in case of illness.

distractors.a: Insurance against theft is voluntary. Health insurance is compulsory.
distractors.c: The Half Fare travelcard (Halbtax) is a voluntary SBB travelcard.

q019.question: What does equality before the law mean?

options.b: All cantons have the same laws.
options.c: All people are equal before the law.
options.d: All people have the same amount of holiday.

q019.why: Equality before the law means that the law applies equally to everyone. Nobody has special privileges before authorities or courts.

distractors.b: Each canton makes its own laws. That is federalism and does not violate equality before the law.
distractors.a: Wages are different. Equality before the law is about how the law treats people, not about income.

q020.question: What are the two «chambers» of the Swiss Parliament called?

options.c: National Council and Council of States

q020.why: The Swiss Parliament consists of two equally strong chambers: the National Council for the people and the Council of States for the cantons.

distractors.b: Senate and Congress are names from other countries, for example from the USA.
distractors.a: Upper House and Lower House are names from Great Britain.
distractors.d: Parliamentary groups and committees are groups within Parliament, not chambers.

q021.question: Switzerland is …
q021.why: In Switzerland the people have the power: they elect Parliament and vote on issues. That is a democracy.

distractors.d: A principality has a prince as head of state. Switzerland has no prince, but its neighbour Liechtenstein is a principality.
distractors.b: In an absolutist state, one ruler has all the power. In Switzerland, power is divided between the people and the authorities.

q022.question: What is an important feature of democracy?

options.d: People have a guaranteed basic income.

q022.why: In a democracy the people have the power. They pass this power on by electing a parliament.

distractors.c: Freedom to travel is a right that can also exist in other forms of government. It is not a feature of democracy.
distractors.d: A guaranteed basic income has nothing to do with the form of government. Switzerland does not have one either.

q023.question: Why are there regular elections in a democracy?

options.a: So that interest in politics is awakened.
options.b: So that the people can decide who represents them.
options.c: So that the poor get more power.
options.d: So that women and men are equally represented.

q023.why: Through elections, the people pass on their power to representatives. Because elections are regular, the people can choose these representatives again and again.

distractors.a: Elections can awaken interest in politics. But their purpose is to choose the people's representatives.
distractors.d: Elections do not guarantee equal representation of women and men. Whoever gets the most votes is elected.

q024.question: What is the constitution of the Swiss Confederation called?
q024.why: Switzerland is a federal state. That is why its constitution is called the Federal Constitution.

distractors.a: The Federal Constitution is the basic law of Switzerland, but «Basic Law» (Grundgesetz) is not its name. That is the name of Germany's constitution.
distractors.c: The Federal Charter of 1291 is an old alliance of the founding cantons, not a constitution.

q025.question: Who runs the government business of Switzerland?
q025.why: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland (executive). That is why it runs the government business.

distractors.d: The Federal Assembly is the parliament. It makes laws and supervises the government, but it does not govern itself.
distractors.a: Parties influence politics, but they do not govern themselves.

q026.question: Who decides on new laws at federal level?

options.c: the National Council, the Council of States and the people (referendum)

q026.why: The National Council and the Council of States pass new laws. With a referendum, the people can then still vote on them and so have the last word.

distractors.a: The Federal Supreme Court applies laws. It does not pass new laws.
distractors.d: The Federal Chancellery supports the Federal Council and organises popular votes. It does not pass laws.

q027.question: Who may vote in elections and popular votes at federal level?

options.c: Swiss citizens who have no criminal record
options.d: people who pay taxes in Switzerland

q027.why: At federal level, two things are needed: Swiss citizenship and an age of 18.

distractors.a: Living in Switzerland is not enough. Foreign nationals in Switzerland may not vote at national level.
distractors.c: A criminal record does not take away your right to vote. There is no such rule.
distractors.d: Foreign nationals also pay taxes. Nevertheless, they may not vote at national level.

q028.question: From what age are Swiss citizens entitled to vote and elect at federal level?
q028.why: At 18 you are of legal age. Since 1991 you may vote and elect at federal level from this age.

distractors.b: 21 years applied in the past. Since the popular vote of 1991 it has been 18 years.
distractors.d: A voting age of 16 exists only in the canton of Glarus, and only for the canton and municipality, not for the Confederation.

q029.question: What does the right to vote (active suffrage) mean in a democracy?

options.a: You may only vote in elections and popular votes if you are active in a political party.
options.b: You can be elected to political office.
options.c: You may vote in elections and popular votes.
options.d: You must help count the votes.

q029.why: «Active» means: you take part yourself and cast your vote. The active right to vote is the right to vote in elections and popular votes.

distractors.b: Being able to be elected is called the passive right to vote (eligibility for election). That is the other side.
distractors.a: You do not have to be in a party to be allowed to vote in elections and popular votes.

q030.question: Who can be elected to political office at federal level?

options.c: anyone who has Swiss citizenship and is of legal age
options.d: anyone who speaks at least two national languages

q030.why: For eligibility for election at federal level, the same rules apply as for the right to vote: Swiss citizenship and at least 18 years of age.

distractors.b: Living in Switzerland is not enough. Without Swiss citizenship, you cannot be elected to a federal political office.
distractors.d: There is no rule that you must speak two national languages to be elected.
distractors.a: Having a job is not a requirement for being elected.

q031.question: How can Swiss citizens influence legislation?

options.a: They can vote on initiatives and referendums.
options.b: They have no direct way of exerting influence.
options.c: They can join a political party.
options.d: They can elect the Federal Council.

q031.why: Initiatives and referendums give the people the last word on the Constitution and laws. That is direct influence on legislation.

distractors.c: In a party you can take part in discussions. But that is only an indirect way. You decide directly with initiatives and referendums.
distractors.d: The Federal Council is elected by the Federal Assembly, not by the people.
distractors.b: Switzerland is a direct democracy. The people have a great deal of direct influence.

q032.question: Against what can a referendum be requested?

options.a: against decisions of the Federal Council
options.b: against judgments of the Federal Supreme Court
options.c: against bills passed by the National Council and the Council of States
options.d: against measures of the Federal Administration

q032.why: A referendum is directed against decisions of Parliament, above all against new laws passed by the National Council and the Council of States.

distractors.a: There is no referendum against decisions and ordinances of the Federal Council.
distractors.b: The people cannot challenge judgments of the Federal Supreme Court with a referendum. The courts are independent.
distractors.d: You can defend yourself against measures of the administration with appeals, not with a referendum.

q033.question: Why is the popular initiative an important political right of voters? With a popular initiative, they can …

options.b: vote the government out of office.
options.d: politically push through important concerns of the population.

q033.why: With an initiative, citizens bring their own topic to a popular vote. This way they can push through concerns that Parliament and the government do not take up.

distractors.c: You stop a decision of Parliament with a referendum. An initiative brings something new.
distractors.b: The Federal Council is elected by the Federal Assembly. The people cannot vote it out of office.
distractors.a: Parliament continues to exist. It debates every initiative and makes a recommendation.

q034.question: How often do voters elect the Federal Parliament?
q034.why: The legislative period lasts four years. After that, the people elect the National Council and the Council of States again.

distractors.a: Six years is the term of office of federal judges, not of Parliament.
distractors.b: Two years would be too short. Parliament is elected every four years.

q035.question: The Federal Assembly has 246 members. Who elects these members?

options.a: the citizens who are entitled to vote

q035.why: In a democracy the people elect the parliament. Swiss citizens aged 18 and over who are entitled to vote may elect.

distractors.c: Foreign nationals may not vote in elections at federal level. Only people entitled to vote with Swiss citizenship elect.
distractors.b: The parties put forward candidates. But the people decide who is elected.

q036.question: At federal level, what can Swiss citizens who are entitled to vote vote on?

options.b: on the radio and television programme schedule
options.d: on filling posts in the administration

q036.why: At federal level, the people vote on popular initiatives and referendums, that is, on amendments to the Constitution and on laws.

distractors.a: Each party decides its own programme. The whole people do not vote on it.
distractors.d: Posts in the administration are filled by the authorities. The people do not elect employees.

q037.question: What is the central task of the Federal Assembly (Federal Parliament)?

options.a: It organises elections and popular votes.
options.c: It runs the government business of Switzerland.
options.d: It delivers court judgments at last instance.

q037.why: Parliament is the legislative power (legislature). Its main task is to debate and pass laws.

distractors.c: Government business is run by the Federal Council, not by Parliament.
distractors.d: Judgments at last instance are delivered by the Federal Supreme Court.
distractors.a: Elections and popular votes are organised by the Federal Chancellery, the cantons and the municipalities, not by Parliament.

q038.question: What is the composition of the United Federal Assembly?

options.a: the members of the National Council and the Council of States
options.c: the members of the cantonal governments

q038.why: The United Federal Assembly is a joint sitting of both chambers. That is why all members of the National Council and the Council of States belong to it.

distractors.b: Federal judges belong to the judiciary, not to Parliament.
distractors.c: The cantonal governments are the executives of the cantons and do not sit in the Federal Parliament.

q039.question: The Federal Palace in Bern is the seat of …
q039.why: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace in Bern. It is the seat of Parliament and also of the Federal Council.

distractors.a: The National Museum is in Zurich, not in the Federal Palace.
distractors.d: Swiss Television has its own studios, mainly in Zurich.

q040.question: What is the executive in Switzerland at federal level called?
q040.why: At federal level, the government, that is the executive, is called the Federal Council.

distractors.a: In some cantons, the cantonal parliament is called the Grand Council (Grosser Rat), for example in Bern.
distractors.d: In some cantons, the cantonal parliament is called the Landrat, for example in Basel-Landschaft.

q041.question: Who elects the seven members of the Federal Council?

options.d: the National Council and the Council of States

q041.why: The members of the Federal Council are elected by the United Federal Assembly, that is, by the National Council and the Council of States together.

distractors.b: The people do not elect the Federal Council directly. They elect Parliament, and Parliament elects the Federal Council.
distractors.a: The parties propose candidates. But the election takes place in Parliament.

q042.question: What function do political parties have in a democracy?

options.a: They represent the various interests and concerns of the population.
options.d: They mediate in disputes between different authorities.

q042.why: Parties bring the concerns of different groups of the population into politics. They put forward candidates and make political proposals.

distractors.b: The Federal Council is elected by the Federal Assembly, not by the parties.
distractors.c: The media in Switzerland are free. Parties do not control them.

q043.question: How many signatures are needed for a popular initiative at federal level?
q043.why: A federal popular initiative needs 100'000 valid signatures, collected within 18 months.

distractors.a: That is too few. A referendum already needs 50'000 signatures, and an initiative needs twice as many.
distractors.c: The law does not require 500'000 signatures. The number is 100'000.

q044.question: What is the task of the Council of States?

options.a: It only has a representative function.
options.b: It is the highest judicial authority.
options.c: It mainly represents the interests of the cantons.
options.d: It coordinates the planning of the municipalities.

q044.why: In the Council of States, each canton has two seats (the six former half-cantons have one each), no matter how many people live there. So the Council of States mainly represents the interests of the cantons.

distractors.a: The Council of States is just as powerful as the National Council. It helps pass laws and does not only have a representative role.
distractors.b: The highest judicial authority is the Federal Supreme Court, not the Council of States.
distractors.d: The Council of States does not plan the municipalities. That is a matter for the cantons and municipalities.

q045.question: What do the National Council and the Council of States do together?

options.b: They elect the members of the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.
options.d: They deliver judgments in the Federal Supreme Court.

q045.why: For certain elections, both chambers meet as the United Federal Assembly. There they elect the Federal Council and the federal judges.

distractors.a: Both chambers decide on important treaties, but each one separately, not together in one sitting.
distractors.c: The budget is drafted by the Federal Council. Parliament then approves it, in separate chambers.
distractors.d: Judgments are delivered by judges, not by members of Parliament.

q046.question: How many times a year do voters normally vote on federal matters?
q046.why: Four Sundays per year are reserved for federal votes. That is the normal number.

distractors.b: Sometimes a date is cancelled because there is no proposal to vote on. But four are planned.
distractors.a: Not five but four Sundays per year are reserved for federal votes.

q046.note: Exam answer: d (4). The learning brochures of the city and canton of Zurich (2024) say «etwa 4 oder 5 Mal im Jahr», probably including cantonal and municipal votes. For the Confederation, the Federal Chancellery reserves four dates per year (bk.admin.ch, 2025).

q047.question: Who decides on a large part of new laws at federal level?

options.c: the National Council and the Council of States

q047.why: Most laws are passed by Parliament and are not put to the people. The people only vote if a referendum is called.

distractors.d: The Federal Council proposes laws and implements them. But Parliament must pass them.
distractors.b: The cantons make cantonal laws. Federal laws are passed by the Federal Parliament.

q047.note: The official German text says «ein Grossteil»; correct German is «einen Grossteil». We show the text as the canton published it.

q048.question: When is an initiative at federal level accepted?

options.a: With a majority of the cantons
options.b: With a majority of the people
options.c: With a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons
options.d: With a majority of the people and at least one third of the cantons

q048.why: A popular initiative amends the Federal Constitution. This always requires both: the majority of votes in the whole country and the majority of the cantons.

distractors.a: The majority of the cantons alone is not enough. The majority of voters must also say yes.
distractors.b: The majority of the people alone is only enough for an optional referendum against a law. An initiative also needs the majority of the cantons.
distractors.d: There is no rule with one third of the cantons. The majority of the cantons is needed.

q049.question: Through a popular initiative …

options.a: the National Council and the Council of States can be removed from office.
options.b: the Federal Constitution can be amended.
options.d: the Federal Council can be replaced.

q049.why: At federal level, a popular initiative always calls for an amendment to the Federal Constitution. Parliament must then implement the new rules.

distractors.c: International law applies between states. Switzerland cannot change it alone, and every initiative must respect mandatory international law.
distractors.d: The Federal Council is elected by the Federal Assembly. An initiative cannot replace it.
distractors.a: The National Council and the Council of States are elected by the people and remain in office until the next elections.

q050.question: How do most voters cast their vote?

options.a: by going to the ballot box

q050.why: The voting documents are sent home by post. Most people fill them in and send them back, because that is simple and convenient.

distractors.a: The ballot box still exists, but only a minority go there in person on Sunday.
distractors.b: E-voting exists only as a trial in a few cantons. The large majority vote by post.

q051.question: On which day of the week do national elections and popular votes take place?
q051.why: Voting Sunday is a tradition. The ballot boxes are open on Sunday, and the results are available in the evening.

distractors.c: On Monday the results are already known. Voting takes place on Sunday.
distractors.b: No national votes take place during the week.

q052.question: What is an important task of the federal state?

options.b: It organises the work in factories and businesses.
options.c: It guarantees affordable housing for everyone.
options.d: It publishes various daily newspapers in all national languages.

q052.why: The important social insurances such as AHV, IV and unemployment insurance are the same throughout the country. The Confederation regulates them and so ensures social security.

distractors.c: The Confederation does not guarantee affordable housing for everyone. Flats are mainly rented out on the free market.
distractors.b: Companies organise the work in factories and businesses themselves. The Confederation only makes rules, for example to protect employees.

q053.question: What is an important task of the Confederation?

options.a: It promotes the founding of associations.
options.b: It supports the founding of companies.
options.c: It ensures internal and external security.
options.d: It runs its own hospitals and clinics.

q053.why: Protecting the whole country is a core task of the Confederation. For this it has, for example, the army and border control.

distractors.d: Hospitals are run by the cantons and municipalities, not by the Confederation.
distractors.b: Companies are founded by private individuals. The Confederation only creates good general conditions for the economy.

q054.question: What is an important task of the Confederation?

options.a: It finances the manufacture of cars.
options.b: It ensures the protection of the environment.
options.c: It sets the key interest rates of the National Bank.
options.d: It runs its own power stations.

q054.why: Environmental problems such as air pollution do not stop at the cantonal border. That is why the Confederation makes laws to protect the environment.

distractors.c: The National Bank sets the key interest rates itself. It is independent of the Federal Council and Parliament.
distractors.d: Power stations mostly belong to cantons, municipalities or companies, not to the Confederation.

q055.question: Which is the Swiss national flag?

options.d: Coat of arms of the canton of Schwyz

q055.why: The Swiss national flag is square and shows a white, even cross in the middle on a red background.

distractors.a: The Danish flag is rectangular, and its white cross is moved to the side.
distractors.b: The Red Cross has the colours reversed: a red cross on a white background.
distractors.d: The coat of arms of Schwyz is red with a small white cross in the upper corner, not in the middle.

q056.question: The Swiss federal state is made up of various. . .
q056.why: The member states of Switzerland are called cantons. Together with the Confederation they form the federal state.

distractors.a: Federal states (Bundesländer) exist in Germany and Austria, not in Switzerland.
distractors.d: Provinces exist, for example, in Italy or Canada. In Switzerland they are called cantons.

q057.question: How many cantons does the Swiss federal state have?
q057.why: Switzerland has 26 cantons. Six of them used to be half-cantons, for example Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft.

distractors.d: 16 is the number of federal states (Bundesländer) in Germany, not the number of cantons in Switzerland.
distractors.a: With 12 cantons there would be less than half as many as there really are.

q057.note: Exam answer: «26 (20 Kantone und 6 Halbkantone)». Today: the Federal Constitution no longer speaks of half-cantons, but of 26 cantons, 6 of which have half a cantonal vote (Federal Constitution Art. 1 and 142, as of 2026).

q058.question: How many political municipalities are there in Switzerland (as of 2021)?
q058.why: Switzerland is divided into a great many small municipalities. In 2021 there were 2172, so about 2200.

distractors.b: 200 municipalities would be far too few. The canton of Zurich alone already has over 150 municipalities.
distractors.d: 8000 is far too many. There are only about 2200, and the number is falling because of municipal mergers.

q058.note: Exam answer: «Etwa 2200» (as of 2021: 2172). Today: 2110 political municipalities (Federal Statistical Office, 1.1.2026).

q059.question: Switzerland is a federal state with three levels of government. What is the lowest level?
q059.why: The municipality is the level closest to the people. That is why it is the lowest of the three levels of government.

distractors.c: Districts exist only in some cantons. They are administrative areas of the canton, not a separate level of government.
distractors.a: The canton is the middle level, between the Confederation and the municipality.

q060.question: Switzerland is a federal state with three levels of government. What is the highest level?
q060.why: The Confederation covers all of Switzerland. That is why it is the highest level of government, above the cantons and municipalities.

distractors.b: The canton is the middle level. The Confederation is above the cantons.
distractors.d: Regions are not a level of government in Switzerland. The three levels are Confederation, canton and municipality.

q061.question: What is the Confederation responsible for?
q061.why: Switzerland acts as one country towards other states. That is why the Confederation is responsible for foreign policy.

distractors.a: State schools are a matter for the cantons and municipalities.
distractors.c: Building regulations are issued by the cantons and municipalities.
distractors.d: Cantonal judges are elected by the canton, usually by the cantonal parliament or by the people.

q062.question: Which level of government is responsible for the military?
q062.why: The army defends all of Switzerland. That is why the Confederation is responsible for the military.

distractors.b: The cantons now only have small tasks in military matters. The army is run by the Confederation.
distractors.d: Municipalities have no army. But they share responsibility, for example, for civil protection.

q063.question: What are the national languages of Switzerland?

options.c: French, Italian, cantonal dialects and Romansh

q063.why: The Federal Constitution names four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.

distractors.a: English is spoken often, but it is not a national language. Romansh is missing.
distractors.c: The dialects are not separate national languages, and German is missing from this list.
distractors.d: Romansh, the fourth national language, is missing here.

q064.question: Which of these is an official national language of Switzerland?
q064.why: French is one of the four national languages. It is spoken in western Switzerland, the Romandie.

distractors.b: English is widespread at work, but it is not a national language.
distractors.c: Many immigrants speak Portuguese, but it is not a national language.

q065.question: How many official national languages are there in Switzerland?
q065.why: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.

distractors.b: Three would be German, French and Italian; but Romansh must be added.

q066.question: What is the fourth national language of Switzerland?
q066.why: Romansh is the fourth and smallest national language. It is spoken in Graubünden.

distractors.a: Alsatian is a German dialect in French Alsace, not a Swiss national language.
distractors.c: English is not a national language of Switzerland.

q067.question: Who is allowed to use force against people and property in Switzerland (monopoly on the use of force)?
q067.why: In Switzerland the state has the monopoly on the use of force. Only state bodies such as the police and the military may use force, according to clear rules. This way the state protects everyone from arbitrariness and revenge.

distractors.a: People who are affected may not use force either. They must turn to the police and the courts. It is only allowed to defend yourself in an acute emergency (self-defence).

q068.question: Who holds judicial power (the judiciary) at federal level?
q068.why: Judicial power lies with the courts. At federal level, the highest court is the Federal Supreme Court.

distractors.a: Members of Parliament make laws (legislature). They do not deliver judgments.
distractors.c: Governments carry out the laws (executive). Judging is a matter for the courts.

q069.question: Who holds legislative power (the legislature) at federal level?

options.c: the Federal Parliament (National Council and Council of States)

q069.why: Laws are debated and passed by the National Council and the Council of States. That is why the Federal Parliament holds legislative power.

distractors.a: The Federal Council is the government, that is, the executive power. It proposes laws, but it does not pass them.
distractors.d: The Federal Supreme Court is the judicial power. It applies laws, but it does not make them.

q070.question: Who holds executive power (the executive) at federal level?

options.c: the Federal Parliament (National Council and Council of States)

q070.why: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It implements the laws that Parliament has passed.

distractors.c: The Federal Parliament is the legislative power (legislature), not the executive power.
distractors.d: The Federal Administrative Court is a court and belongs to the judicial power (judiciary).

q071.question: What is often referred to as the fourth power in the state?
q071.why: The media inform the population and criticise politics and the authorities. Because they control power in this way, they are often called the fourth power.

distractors.b: Associations and clubs represent interests and influence politics. But it is the media that are called the fourth power.
distractors.a: The church has no state power in Switzerland and is not considered the fourth power.

q072.question: What is the task of judges?
q072.why: Courts are the judicial power. Judges decide cases according to the law and deliver judgments.

distractors.c: The accused are defended by lawyers. Judges must remain impartial.
distractors.d: Laws are made by Parliament, not by the courts.
distractors.a: The administration is mainly supervised by Parliament. Courts only examine individual cases.

q073.question: What is a task of the police?

options.b: It prosecutes violations of the law.

q073.why: The police ensure security. When someone breaks a law, they investigate and look for the offenders.

distractors.d: Judgments are delivered by the courts. The police only investigate.
distractors.c: Laws are issued by Parliament, not by the police.

q074.question: Who is allowed to arrest criminals?
q074.why: Because of the monopoly on the use of force, making arrests is the task of the state, that is, of the police. Private persons may at most hold someone briefly in an emergency until the police arrive.

distractors.a: Witnesses should call the police and give evidence, but not make arrests themselves.
distractors.b: The municipal council is a political authority. Arrests are made by the police.
distractors.d: A vigilante group is not a state body and may not use force.

q075.question: What does separation of powers mean?

options.a: The police and the military may both use force.
options.b: The distribution of power between state and church.
options.c: The distribution of state power among different state bodies such as the government, parliament and the courts.
options.d: The distribution of power between the National Council and the Council of States.

q075.why: Separation of powers means that state power is divided among parliament, government and the courts. This way no single body can have all the power.

distractors.a: Here «power» (Gewalt) does not mean physical force, but state power.
distractors.d: The National Council and the Council of States are both part of the same power, the legislature.
distractors.b: The separation of state and church is a different topic. Separation of powers concerns the state bodies.

q076.question: Switzerland is a state governed by the rule of law. What does that mean?

options.a: The state, too, must abide by the laws.
options.b: The laws only apply to the people who agreed to these laws.
options.c: The laws only apply to Swiss citizens.
options.d: The laws do not apply to politicians.

q076.why: In a state governed by the rule of law, the laws are above everyone. The authorities, the government and the police must also abide by them and may not act arbitrarily.

distractors.b: Laws apply to everyone, including people who voted no.
distractors.c: The laws apply to all people in Switzerland, not only to Swiss citizens.
distractors.d: Politicians must also abide by the laws. Nobody is above the law.

q077.question: Which fundamental right is enshrined in the Federal Constitution?

options.d: the right to a house of one's own

q077.why: Freedom of religion and conscience protects religion and personal beliefs. It is in the Federal Constitution.

distractors.a: Owning weapons is regulated by law, but it is not a fundamental right.
distractors.d: The state does not guarantee anyone a house of their own. What is protected is the property you already have.

q078.question: Which fundamental right does the Federal Constitution guarantee?

options.c: the right to free education and continuing education

q078.why: Freedom of opinion is a central fundamental right. Without it, there would be no free discussion before elections and popular votes.

distractors.c: Only compulsory school is free of charge. There is no fundamental right to free education and continuing education.
distractors.b: Internet and Wi-Fi are not a fundamental right.

q079.question: What is guaranteed by freedom of religion and conscience?
q079.why: «Glauben» (belief) means religion. Freedom of religion and conscience guarantees that every person may freely choose and practise their religion.

distractors.c: Freedom of assembly is also a fundamental right, but a different one. It is in a separate article.
distractors.a: There is no free choice of school in state schools. Children go to school where they live.

q080.question: According to the Constitution and the law, women and men in Switzerland have equal rights. What does that mean?

options.b: Women and men have fundamentally the same rights.
options.c: Political bodies must have as many men as women.
options.d: Bringing up children is women's business.

q080.why: Equal rights means the same rights for women and men, for example in the family, at work and in politics.

distractors.c: Switzerland has no fixed quota for political bodies. Equal rights means equal rights, not equal numbers.

q081.question: What is prohibited in Switzerland?

options.a: You may not publicly spread false claims about people.
options.b: You may not publicly criticise the government.
options.c: You may not dissolve a marriage once it has been concluded.
options.d: You may not take part in demonstrations.

q081.why: Anyone who publicly spreads false claims about a person damages their reputation. This is punishable as defamation or slander.

distractors.b: Freedom of opinion allows criticism of the government. That is part of democracy.
distractors.c: A marriage can be dissolved by divorce.
distractors.d: Demonstrations are protected by freedom of assembly. Often a permit is needed.

q082.question: Someone does not get a job because of their skin colour or their sex. Which fundamental right is violated?

options.a: the right to freedom of expression
options.c: the right to equal treatment (prohibition of discrimination)

q082.why: Anyone who is disadvantaged because of their skin colour or sex is discriminated against. The Federal Constitution prohibits this.

distractors.a: Freedom of expression protects the right to say what you think. This case is about unequal treatment.
distractors.b: Freedom of domicile means that Swiss citizens may live anywhere in Switzerland. That does not fit this case.

q083.question: Which right do people only receive through naturalisation?

options.b: They may take part in political elections and popular votes at federal level.
options.d: They may freely choose their job.

q083.why: The right to vote and elect at federal level is reserved for Swiss citizens. Foreign nationals already have the other rights mentioned before naturalisation.

distractors.a: Any person may join an association. You do not need a Swiss passport for that.
distractors.c: Foreign nationals living in Switzerland may buy a flat that they live in themselves.
distractors.d: Many foreign nationals may already choose their job freely with their permit, without naturalisation.

q084.question: What violates personal privacy or data protection?

options.a: When a personal computer is not sufficiently protected.
options.b: When a person is photographed on a public street.
options.c: When a newspaper reports on a person.
options.d: When private information about individual people is published without a legal basis or without the person's consent.

q084.why: Private information belongs to the person themselves. Anyone who publishes it without consent or a legal basis violates their privacy.

distractors.b: Being photographed on the street is not automatically prohibited. It only becomes a problem when private pictures are published without consent.
distractors.c: Newspapers may report on people. But they must respect their privacy.
distractors.a: A badly protected computer is a risk, but it is not yet a violation of data protection by others.

q085.question: What does the Swiss Federal Constitution prohibit?

options.a: You may not wear religious symbols in public spaces.
options.b: You may not run collections for people in need.
options.d: You may not work without pay.

q085.why: The Federal Constitution protects human dignity. Torture is therefore prohibited without any exception.

distractors.a: In principle you may wear religious symbols such as a cross or a headscarf. Freedom of religion protects this.
distractors.d: Voluntary work without pay is allowed, for example in an association.
distractors.b: Collections for people in need are allowed.

q086.question: Which right is enshrined in the Swiss Federal Constitution?

options.a: All people have a right to healthy and free food.
options.d: You may use the internet free of charge.

q086.why: The guarantee of ownership protects what belongs to a person. The state may not simply take it away.

distractors.a: People in need receive help for the bare necessities. But there is no right to free food for everyone.
distractors.d: Free internet is not a right in the Federal Constitution.

q087.question: What is prohibited in Switzerland?

options.a: criticising the work of the Federal Council
options.b: riding a bicycle without a permit
options.c: wearing a religious symbol in public spaces
options.d: publicly insulting other people because of their origin or religion

q087.why: Anyone who publicly insults people because of their origin or religion violates their dignity. This is punishable as discrimination and incitement to hatred.

distractors.a: Criticising the Federal Council is allowed and is part of democracy.
distractors.c: In principle you may wear religious symbols. Freedom of religion protects this.

q088.question: Who must do military service or civil protection service in Switzerland?

options.b: women and men aged 20 who have lived in Switzerland for at least 10 years
options.c: military service is voluntary for everyone
options.d: young women and men with a technical or medical profession

q088.why: The obligation to serve applies to Swiss men. They do military service, civilian service or civil protection service.

distractors.b: Women have no obligation to serve, and the length of residence does not matter. Swiss citizenship is what counts.
distractors.c: Service is compulsory for Swiss men. It is voluntary only for women.
distractors.d: The profession does not matter. Women can serve voluntarily.

q089.question: Two young people are not let into the swimming pool because of their dark skin colour. Which fundamental right does this violate?
q089.why: The young people are treated worse because of their skin colour. That is exactly what the prohibition of discrimination forbids.

distractors.d: Freedom of assembly protects meetings and demonstrations. This case is about disadvantage because of skin colour.
distractors.a: A «freedom to do sport» does not exist as a fundamental right. The problem is the unequal treatment.

q090.question: Which obligation applies only to men in Switzerland?

options.a: Men must do military service or civil protection service up to a certain age.
options.b: Men must take on a political office if needed.
options.c: Men must provide for the family's maintenance.
options.d: Men must pay more taxes and health insurance premiums.

q090.why: The Federal Constitution obliges only Swiss men to do military service. For women it is voluntary.

distractors.b: There is no obligation only for men to take on a political office.
distractors.c: Both parents provide for the family's maintenance together.
distractors.d: Taxes and health insurance premiums do not depend on sex.

q091.question: What is prohibited in a state governed by the rule of law?

options.b: questioning the work of democratically elected authorities
options.c: arresting and imprisoning people without reason

q091.why: In a state governed by the rule of law, the state is also bound by the laws. It may not arrest or imprison anyone without reason and without a regulated procedure.

distractors.a: Criticising laws is allowed. Freedom of opinion protects this.
distractors.b: You may question the work of the authorities. Criticism is part of democracy.
distractors.d: Freedom of religion allows you to join a religious group.

q092.question: What happens in Switzerland when someone commits a criminal offence?

options.a: Anyone who has broken a law is punished.
options.b: Anyone who has become the victim of a crime may take revenge themselves.
options.c: Anyone who reports themselves goes unpunished.
options.d: The victims of a crime can choose between different punishments.

q092.why: In a state governed by the rule of law, the law applies to everyone. Anyone who commits a criminal offence is prosecuted, and a court decides the punishment according to the law.

distractors.b: Taking the law into your own hands is prohibited. Only the state may punish (monopoly on the use of force).
distractors.c: Reporting yourself can reduce the punishment, but as a rule it does not mean you go unpunished.
distractors.d: The punishment is decided by the court according to the law, not by the victim.

q093.question: Which punishment does the Federal Constitution prohibit?
q093.why: The Federal Constitution protects the right to life. That is why the death penalty is prohibited.

distractors.a: Prison sentences are allowed and are regulated in the Criminal Code.
distractors.d: Community service is an allowed way of serving a sentence.

q094.question: There are various laws in Switzerland. Which one governs the renting of flats?

options.d: Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy (SchKG)

q094.why: Renting is a contract. Contracts are governed by the law of obligations; tenancy law is found there.

distractors.c: The StGB governs criminal offences and punishments, not contracts.
distractors.d: The SchKG helps to collect debts, for example unpaid rent. It does not govern the tenancy agreement itself.

q095.question: There are various laws in Switzerland. What does the Civil Code (ZGB) govern?
q095.why: The ZGB governs the lives of persons and families. This includes marriage and divorce.

distractors.b: The founding of companies is in the Code of Obligations (OR).
distractors.c: Punishments for murder and manslaughter are in the Criminal Code (StGB).

q096.question: There are various laws in Switzerland. Which one governs whether someone has to go to prison?

options.d: Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy (SchKG)

q096.why: Prison is a punishment. Which acts are punishable and which punishments exist for them is governed by the Criminal Code.

distractors.d: Nobody goes to prison because of debts alone. The SchKG only governs debt enforcement.
distractors.a: The OR governs contracts, not punishments.
distractors.b: The ZGB governs family and persons, not punishments.

q097.question: How are the judges of the Federal Supreme Court appointed?

options.a: By the cantonal parliaments. Each canton can provide one judge.
options.b: Through a normal application process with a job interview.
options.c: By election by the Federal Parliament.
options.d: The Federal Council has the right to appoint judges.

q097.why: Federal judges are elected by the United Federal Assembly, that is, by the National Council and the Council of States together, for six years.

distractors.d: The Federal Council is the government. Because of the separation of powers, it may not appoint judges.
distractors.b: You can apply, but in the end an election in Parliament decides, not a job interview.
distractors.a: The cantons only elect their own cantonal judges. Federal judges are elected by the Federal Parliament.

q098.question: May Swiss citizens be extradited to other countries?

options.a: No. This is not permitted under any circumstances.
options.b: Yes, but only to countries that are democratically organised.
options.c: Yes, but only if the offence is also punishable in Switzerland.
options.d: In principle, no. Exceptions apply for trials before international courts.

q098.why: The Federal Constitution protects Swiss citizens from being extradited to another state against their will. But international criminal courts are not a foreign state; Switzerland can hand over its own citizens to them.

distractors.a: It is not completely ruled out. There is an exception for international courts.
distractors.b: Switzerland does not extradite its own citizens against their will, not even to democratic states.
distractors.c: For foreign nationals, the offence also being punishable in Switzerland is only one of several conditions. The Constitution protects Swiss citizens more strongly.

q098.note: Exam answer: d. Today: Swiss citizens may be extradited to another state if they themselves agree (Federal Constitution Art. 25, as of 2025).

q099.question: What does an individual's tax burden depend on?

options.b: on membership of a political party

q099.why: Taxes are based on economic capacity. Taxable income and assets are what count.

distractors.c: Nationality does not determine the amount of tax. For foreign nationals with certain permits, only the way the tax is collected changes (withholding tax).

q100.question: How many members does the Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat) of the canton of Zurich have?
q100.why: The Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat) has 7 members. Each one heads one of the 7 directorates of the cantonal administration.

distractors.d: 180 is the number of members of the Cantonal Council (Kantonsrat), that is, the parliament.
distractors.a: With only 3 members, the many tasks of the canton could not be divided up.

q101.question: What is the name of a directorate of the canton of Zurich?
q101.why: The Directorate of Building is one of the 7 directorates. It is responsible, for example, for cantonal roads, waters and the environment.

distractors.d: The military is a matter for the Confederation, so the canton of Zurich has no Directorate of Military Affairs.
distractors.a: Tourism belongs to the Directorate of Economic Affairs; there is no separate Directorate of Tourism.

q102.question: What is the executive called in the city of Zurich?
q102.why: In the city of Zurich, the government is called the City Council (Stadtrat). It has 9 members and heads the city administration.

distractors.c: The Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat) is the government of the canton, not of the city.
distractors.d: The Federal Council is the government of all of Switzerland.

q103.question: What is a task of the canton of Zurich?

options.a: Concluding treaties with the European Union

q103.why: The University of Zurich is a cantonal university. Universities are among the tasks of the canton.

distractors.a: Treaties with the EU are concluded by the Confederation, because foreign policy is a federal matter.
distractors.d: The army is a matter for the Confederation.
distractors.c: The Confederation organises the Federal Administration itself.

q104.question: How many districts are there in the canton of Zurich?
q104.why: The canton of Zurich is divided into 12 districts, for example Zurich, Winterthur, Uster and Horgen.

distractors.c: 7 is the number of members of the Cantonal Government, not the number of districts.

q105.question: How can people without a Swiss passport also become politically active in the canton of Zurich?

options.c: with a seat in the government.
options.d: with a motion in a parliamentary committee.

q105.why: Any person may submit a petition, even without a Swiss passport. The authority must examine it.

distractors.a: Only people entitled to vote, that is, Swiss citizens, can sign a referendum.
distractors.d: Only elected members of parliament may submit motions in parliament.

q106.question: How many members does the government of the canton of Zurich have?

options.d: depending on the tasks at hand.

q106.why: The Zurich government is the Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat). It always has 7 members.

distractors.c: The number is fixed in the constitution: 7, not 5.
distractors.d: The number does not change depending on the tasks. It is fixed.

q107.question: What are the cantons mainly responsible for?

options.a: for running the cantonal administration and for cantonal laws
options.b: for domestic and foreign policy at national level
options.d: for monetary policy and customs duties

q107.why: The cantons have their own laws and their own administration, which is headed by the Cantonal Government.

distractors.b: National domestic and foreign policy is made by the Confederation.
distractors.c: The military is a matter for the Confederation.
distractors.d: Monetary policy (National Bank) and customs duties are tasks of the Confederation.

q108.question: How often are the members of the Cantonal Council (Kantonsrat) elected?
q108.why: The Cantonal Council (Kantonsrat) is elected every 4 years, just like the Cantonal Government.

distractors.a: In Switzerland, terms of office of 4 years are usual, not 6.
distractors.c: 7 is the number of members of the Cantonal Government, not a term of office.

q109.question: What is the executive called in the canton of Zurich?
q109.why: The executive is the government. In the canton of Zurich it is called the Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat).

distractors.c: The Council of States is a chamber of the Federal Parliament, so it is legislative and not cantonal.
distractors.a: In some other cantons, the person who chairs the government is called the Landammann.

q110.question: Which is the coat of arms of the canton of Zurich?

options.a: Coat of arms of the canton of Lucerne (vertical)
options.b: Coat of arms of the canton of Zug
options.c: Coat of arms of the canton of Zurich
options.d: Coat of arms of the canton of Ticino

q110.why: The correct coat of arms is divided diagonally: white at the top right, blue at the bottom left; the line runs from top left to bottom right. The Zurich coat of arms has looked like this since the 14th century.

distractors.a: The coat of arms divided vertically into blue and white belongs to Lucerne. In the Zurich coat of arms the division is diagonal.
distractors.b: White with a blue horizontal bar is the coat of arms of Zug. It has the same colours, but no diagonal line.
distractors.d: The coat of arms with red and blue belongs to Ticino. Zurich has no red in its coat of arms.

q111.question: How many people represent the canton of Zurich in the Council of States?
q111.why: In the Council of States, each full canton has 2 seats, regardless of its size. That is why Zurich also has only 2.

distractors.d: 7 is the number of members of the Zurich Cantonal Government.
distractors.a: Zurich has many seats in the National Council, not in the Council of States.

q112.question: What is the parliament of the canton of Zurich called?
q112.why: The parliament of the canton of Zurich is called the Cantonal Council (Kantonsrat) and has 180 members.

distractors.b: «Grand Council» (Grosser Rat) is the name of the parliament in other cantons, for example in Bern or Aargau.
distractors.d: The Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat) is the government, not the parliament.
distractors.a: Landtag is the name of the parliament in Germany and Liechtenstein.

q113.question: How are the members of the Zurich government chosen?

options.a: They are appointed by the political parties.
options.b: They are elected by the Cantonal Council.
options.c: They are elected at party meetings.
options.d: They are elected by the voters of Zurich.

q113.why: The people elect the Cantonal Government directly, every 4 years, in a majority election.

distractors.b: The Cantonal Council does not elect the government. This is different from the Federal Council, which is elected by Parliament.
distractors.a: Parties propose candidates, but the people elect.

q114.question: Who issues driving licences for car drivers in the canton of Zurich?
q114.why: The Road Traffic Office is an office of the canton. It holds the driving tests and issues driving licences.

distractors.d: The traffic police check the traffic, but they do not issue driving licences.
distractors.a: The municipality is not responsible for cars and driving licences.

q115.question: Who may register motor vehicles for use on the road?
q115.why: The Road Traffic Office inspects vehicles and registers them for use on the road. Then you get the number plates.

distractors.b: Garages sell and repair cars, but they may not register them.
distractors.d: The police check vehicles on the road, but they do not register them.

q116.question: How are the members of the Cantonal Council chosen?

options.b: through appointment by the cantonal government
options.d: by the canton's members of the Council of States

q116.why: The people elect the 180 members of the Cantonal Council every 4 years in a proportional election.

distractors.b: The government does not appoint the parliament, because the parliament is supposed to supervise the government.
distractors.d: The members of the Council of States represent the canton in Bern; they do not decide who sits in the Cantonal Council.

q117.question: What happens at a municipal assembly (Gemeindeversammlung)?

options.a: The voters decide on the budget.
options.c: The voters elect the head of the fire service.
options.d: The voters pass new national laws.

q117.why: At the municipal assembly, the people entitled to vote decide directly on important matters, for example on the budget.

distractors.d: National laws are passed by the Federal Parliament, not by the municipality.
distractors.c: The head of the fire service is not elected at the municipal assembly, but appointed by the authorities.

q118.question: Who elects the City Parliament (Gemeinderat) of the city of Zurich?
q118.why: In the city of Zurich, the Gemeinderat is the City Parliament. Its 125 members are elected by the people.

distractors.a: The Cantonal Council is the parliament of the canton. It does not elect a city parliament.
distractors.b: The Cantonal Government is the government of the canton and does not appoint a parliament.
