q185.why: In marriage, wife and husband have equal rights. That is why each person can file for divorce, or both together.

distractors.a: Wife and husband have the same rights. Not only the husband may ask for a divorce.
distractors.d: The husband may also ask for a divorce, not only the wife.

q186.question: Who must register the intention to marry at the civil registry office?
q186.why: The couple registers together at the civil registry office. Both must declare that they want to marry.

distractors.a: Woman and man have equal rights. Both must declare their wish to marry.
distractors.b: The parents play no role. The engaged couple is of legal age and decides for themselves.

q187.question: Whom must you let into your own flat upon a justified request?

options.c: people who are standing for a public office in the municipality

q187.why: The landlord may enter the flat for a good reason, for example for repairs or viewings. He must announce this in advance.

distractors.a: The postal worker brings the post to the door. You do not have to let her into the flat.
distractors.d: The employer has no right to come into your private flat.

q188.question: What is the Tenants' Association (Mieterinnen- und Mieterverband)?

options.a: a federal conciliation authority for tenancy matters
options.c: an organisation representing the interests of tenants
options.d: an association of all tenants in Switzerland

q188.why: The Tenants' Association represents the interests of tenants. It advises members and does politics for them.

distractors.a: The conciliation authority is a state body. The association is a private association.
distractors.d: Membership is voluntary. Not all tenants belong to it.

q189.question: What is a requirement for getting married in Switzerland?

options.a: Both partners must be at least 16 years old.
options.b: The partners must already be living in a registered partnership.
options.c: The partners must have the same place of residence.
options.d: The partners may not be closely related.

q189.why: Close relatives may not marry each other, that is parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or brothers and sisters.

distractors.a: The minimum age for marriage is 18, not 16.
distractors.c: You do not already have to live together to be allowed to marry.

q190.question: When can a driving licence be withdrawn?

options.a: for unauthorised use of the horn
options.b: for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs

q190.why: Anyone who drives under the influence of alcohol or drugs puts others in serious danger. That is why the driving licence can be withdrawn.

distractors.c: Parking incorrectly costs a fine, but the licence is not withdrawn for it.
distractors.d: In fog, you must drive slowly and carefully. But driving is not prohibited.

q191.question: What surname does a child of married parents receive?

options.a: always a double name with the mother's name first
options.d: must be decided at the wedding by parents without a common family name

q191.why: If the parents have no common family name, they decide at the wedding which of their maiden names the children will have.

distractors.b: Since 2013, the father's name is no longer automatically the children's name.
distractors.a: Double names do not exist for children. The child gets a single name.

q191.note: Exam answer: «Die Eltern ohne gemeinsamen Namen entscheiden bei der Heirat». This still applies. In 2026, Parliament decided to allow double names for married couples again; but children will still only get one name (date of entry into force still open).

q192.question: Dog owners must, for their dog, …
q192.why: Dog owners must pay a dog tax to the municipality every year.

distractors.d: Health insurance for dogs is voluntary. But in the canton of Zurich you need liability insurance for your dog.
distractors.a: Giving a dog a name is usual, but not an obligation. The dog tax is an obligation.

q193.question: When can someone receive so-called supplementary benefits?

options.a: When you have an apprenticeship at a company.
options.b: When you do not reach the minimum wage.
options.c: When, despite an IV or AHV pension, you do not reach the subsistence minimum.

q193.why: Supplementary benefits are paid if the AHV or IV pension is not enough for the subsistence minimum. They add to the pension.

distractors.b: Supplementary benefits (EL) do not make up for a low wage. They are mainly paid in addition to an AHV or IV pension.
distractors.d: If you are unemployed, unemployment insurance pays, not supplementary benefits.

q194.question: Where is membership compulsory in Switzerland?

options.d: in an automobile club or cycling club

q194.why: Basic insurance with a health insurance fund is compulsory for everyone.

distractors.a: Membership of a party is voluntary. There is freedom of association.

q195.question: Who may found an association?

options.a: only people with a record of sporting achievement
options.b: only people above a certain income
options.d: all women and men aged 21 and over

q195.why: Freedom of association is a fundamental right. That is why every person in Switzerland may found an association.

distractors.d: There is no minimum age of 21 for founding an association. You are already of legal age at 18.

q196.question: Which of these is one of the most important cantonal and municipal taxes?
q196.why: The canton and the municipality tax wealth, that is savings and property. This is one of their most important taxes.

distractors.b: Tobacco tax is levied by the Confederation, not by the canton or the municipality.

q197.question: Which of these is one of the most important cantonal and municipal taxes?
q197.why: Income tax on wages is the most important source of revenue for the canton and the municipality.

distractors.a: Withholding tax on interest is levied by the Confederation.
distractors.b: Alcohol tax is levied by the Confederation.
distractors.c: Customs duties are a matter for the Confederation.

q198.question: Who is primarily responsible for state schools in Switzerland?
q198.why: Compulsory state school is a matter for the cantons. The municipalities organise the schools locally.

distractors.a: There is no federal school administration for compulsory state school. The Confederation is hardly responsible here.
distractors.c: The cantons work together (in the EDK), but each canton is responsible itself.

q199.question: When does compulsory schooling begin in the canton of Zurich?
q199.why: In the canton of Zurich, kindergarten is compulsory. So compulsory schooling begins with kindergarten, usually at the age of 4.

distractors.b: Primary school is already the second stage. Before it come 2 compulsory years of kindergarten.
distractors.c: Playgroup is voluntary and is not part of compulsory state school.

q200.question: What is a neighbourhood association (Quartierverein)?

options.a: An association that regulates the rights of a neighbourhood vis-à-vis the Confederation and the canton.
options.b: An association that stands up for the interests of a neighbourhood's residents vis-à-vis the authorities and promotes social life.
options.c: An association of which the residents of a neighbourhood are automatically members.
options.d: An association that regulates the traffic routes within a neighbourhood and checks compliance with the traffic rules.

q200.why: A neighbourhood association stands up for the people in the neighbourhood towards the authorities and organises joint events.

distractors.c: Membership is voluntary. No one is automatically a member.
distractors.a: An association does not regulate any rights towards the Confederation and the canton. It can only represent concerns.
distractors.d: Traffic rules are checked by the police, not by an association.

q201.question: What is the purpose of financial equalisation between the municipalities?

options.a: It is meant to help fight corruption.
options.b: It is meant to help avoid inflation.
options.c: It forces poor municipalities to fulfil their obligations (schools, old people's homes, etc.).
options.d: It supports poor municipalities or municipalities with high social expenditure in carrying out their tasks.

q201.why: Financial equalisation gives money to poorer municipalities or municipalities with high social costs, so that they can carry out their tasks.

distractors.c: Financial equalisation does not force anyone. It gives support with money.
distractors.b: Inflation is fought by the National Bank, not by financial equalisation.

q202.question: What support does the municipality provide if your own income or assets are not sufficient to cover living costs?
q202.why: Anyone who does not have enough money to live on can apply to the municipality for social assistance.

distractors.b: «Gemeinderappen» is not a term for state support.
distractors.d: «Cantonal money» does not exist. The support is called social assistance.

q203.question: Where can you find information about the municipality's services and regulations?

options.a: in the local newspaper or on the internet
options.c: on the notice board in the shopping centre

q203.why: The municipality publishes its information on its website and in the local newspaper, often in the official section.

distractors.b: Television rarely reports on the services of individual municipalities.
distractors.d: Posters mainly show advertising, not official information.

q204.question: Which social benefits do the municipalities pay for?

options.d: Travel costs in your free time

q204.why: The municipalities pay social assistance for people in an emergency situation. The canton contributes to it.

distractors.b: The old-age pension comes from the AHV, a federal insurance.
distractors.c: Each person pays the costs of the driving test themselves.

q205.question: Who is responsible for financing and organising primary school?

options.b: the canton together with the municipalities

q205.why: The canton and the municipalities finance and organise primary school together. It is free for parents.

distractors.c: The Confederation is not responsible for compulsory state school.
distractors.a: State school is free. Parents do not pay for it directly.

q206.question: Where must you go if you want to get married?
q206.why: The civil registry office checks whether a marriage is allowed and performs the wedding ceremony.

distractors.d: Marriage counselling helps with problems in a marriage. It is not responsible for getting married.

q207.question: Where must you register when you move?
q207.why: When you move, you deregister at the residents' registration office of your municipality and register in the new municipality.

distractors.a: The tax office gets your address automatically from the municipality. You do not register there.
distractors.b: The police are not responsible for registering residents.

q208.question: Who runs the state schools in Zurich municipalities?
q208.why: The school management runs the school day to day: it leads the teachers and organises how the school works.

distractors.c: The school secretariat does administrative work. It does not run the school.
distractors.d: The teachers take part, but they do not run the school.

q209.question: In 1798, a European ruler briefly turned the Confederation into a centralised state. What was the ruler's name?
q209.why: Napoleon is the best-known French ruler of that time. In 1798, France turned Switzerland into the Helvetic Republic, a centralised state.

distractors.a: Rudolf of Habsburg lived in the 13th century, at the time of the founding cantons.
distractors.c: Charles the Bold of Burgundy lost against the Confederates in the 15th century (Grandson, Murten).

q209.note: Exam answer: «Napoleon Bonaparte» (the learning brochures say so too). Today: in 1798, France was ruled by the Directory; Napoleon was a general at that time. He ruled from 1799 and ended the centralised state in 1803 with the Act of Mediation (HLS, «Helvetische Republik»).

q210.question: Who played an important role in founding the Federal Institute of Technology (ETH), in building the railways and in founding today's Credit Suisse?
q210.why: Alfred Escher shaped modern Switzerland in the 19th century. He promoted railway building, helped found the ETH and founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt.

distractors.a: Conrad Ferdinand Meyer was a Zurich poet, not an entrepreneur.
distractors.b: Robert Grimm was a Social Democrat and led the national general strike in 1918.
distractors.c: General Henri Dufour led the army in the Sonderbund War and directed the work on the first accurate map of Switzerland (Dufour map).

q210.note: Exam answer: «Alfred Escher». Today: Credit Suisse no longer exists as a separate bank. It was taken over by UBS in 2023 (Federal Council, 2023).

q211.question: During the national general strike (Landesstreik) of 1918, workers demanded more rights. What was one consequence of the national strike?

options.b: Workers could travel to work by train free of charge.

q211.why: The 48-hour week was one of the nine demands of the national general strike. It was introduced as early as 1919; before that, many people worked almost 60 hours a week.

distractors.c: Holidays were not a main demand; even today, there is no legal right to 6 weeks of holiday in Switzerland.
distractors.d: The factories stayed in private hands; Switzerland did not nationalise its industry.

q212.question: What did the so-called «Schwarzenbach initiative» of 1970 demand?

options.a: the introduction of English lessons in primary school
options.d: a limit on the number of foreigners

q212.why: The initiative wanted to limit the number of foreigners in each canton except Geneva to at most 10 percent. It was narrowly rejected in 1970.

distractors.b: The minaret ban was a different initiative and was accepted in 2009.

q213.question: What is the significance of the year 1848 in Swiss history?

options.a: Founding of the Swiss federal state
options.b: Guarantee of neutrality by the European powers
options.c: Defeat of Confederate troops at Marignano
options.d: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire

q213.why: On 12 September 1848, the first Federal Constitution entered into force. This created the Swiss federal state as we know it today.

distractors.b: Neutrality was already recognised by the European powers in 1815.
distractors.c: The defeat at Marignano was in 1515.
distractors.d: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised in 1648 in the Peace of Westphalia.

q214.question: What is the Swiss national anthem called?
q214.why: The anthem is called «Swiss Psalm» because it sounds like a religious song (psalm). It has been the official national anthem since 1981.

distractors.b: «Hallelujah» is a well-known religious song, but not the Swiss anthem.

q215.question: Which canton has only been an independent canton since 1979?
q215.why: From 1815, the Jura belonged to the canton of Bern. After a long dispute, it became the 26th canton of Switzerland on 1 January 1979.

distractors.a: St. Gallen has been a canton since 1803.
distractors.d: Solothurn has been part of the Confederation since 1481.

q216.question: In the 16th century there was an important religious movement in Europe and in Switzerland. What is it called?
q216.why: The Reformation was a Christian movement that wanted to renew the Catholic Church. In Switzerland, it was led by Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva.

distractors.c: Scepticism is a school of philosophical thought, not a religious movement.

q217.question: When did Swiss women obtain the right to vote and elect at federal level?
q217.why: On 7 February 1971, Swiss men said yes at the ballot box. Since then, women have been allowed to vote and elect at federal level.

distractors.a: In 1918, the national general strike demanded women's suffrage, but it was not introduced at that time.
distractors.c: In 1948, the AHV was introduced, not women's suffrage.

q218.question: In the 1950s, Switzerland needed foreign workers. Where did most of them come from?
q218.why: In 1948, Switzerland concluded an agreement with Italy on workers. That is why mainly Italians came in the 1950s.

distractors.a: People from Portugal came mainly later, in the 1980s and 1990s.
distractors.b: Fewer people came from France; Italy was by far the most important country of origin.

q219.question: Why did many people come to Switzerland from (former) Yugoslavia in the 1990s?

options.a: They wanted to study at a Swiss university.
options.b: They wanted to visit their relatives and travel around Switzerland.
options.c: They were fleeing the war in their home country.
options.d: They were needed as workers for the Grande Dixence dam project.

q219.why: In the 1990s, there were wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Kosovo. That is why many people fled to Switzerland.

distractors.d: Workers came earlier for dams such as Grande Dixence, mainly from Italy; people from the former Yugoslavia fled the war in the 1990s.

q220.question: How can Switzerland's relationship with the warring powers in the Second World War be described?

options.c: neutral, with political and economic relations with the warring powers
options.d: neutral, with no relations with the warring powers

q220.why: Switzerland remained neutral and did not fight. But it had political and economic relations with both sides, especially trade with Germany.

distractors.d: It was not possible without any relations: Switzerland needed coal and food and supplied goods to both sides.
distractors.a: Switzerland was not allied with either side, not even with the Allies.
distractors.b: Switzerland was not an ally of the Axis powers, even though it traded a lot with Germany.

q221.question: In Switzerland, industrialisation began in the early 19th century. What was most important in this process?
q221.why: In Switzerland, industrialisation began with the spinning and weaving of cotton. In 1802, the first large mechanical spinning mill opened near Winterthur.

distractors.b: Switzerland has hardly any iron ore; the steel industry was never the core of Swiss industry.
distractors.c: There is almost no coal in Switzerland; it had to be imported.

q222.question: Men and women have equal rights. Since when has this sentence been in the Constitution?
q222.why: On 14 June 1981, the people and the cantons accepted the equality article. It also requires equal pay for work of equal value.

distractors.c: The Gender Equality Act entered into force in 1996; the sentence had already been in the Constitution since 1981.

q223.question: In the 19th century, Switzerland changed ...

options.a: from a federal state into a centralised state.
options.d: from an agrarian state into an industrial state.

q223.why: Around 1800, most people lived from agriculture. By 1900, many worked in factories: Switzerland became an industrial state.

distractors.a: It was the other way round: in 1848 Switzerland became a federal state, not a centralised state.
distractors.c: Switzerland never had colonies of its own.

q224.question: When did the standard of living in Switzerland rise significantly for many people?
q224.why: After the Second World War, the economy grew strongly. In the 1960s, wages rose particularly fast, and many people could afford a car, a television and holidays.

distractors.a: Around 1900, many working-class families still lived in poverty and worked very long hours.
distractors.b: In the 1930s, there was the Great Depression with high unemployment.

q225.question: During Europe's colonial rule ...

options.a: Switzerland had colonies in Asia and Africa.
options.b: Swiss mercenaries were active in Russia.
options.c: Switzerland exported spices to North America.
options.d: Switzerland was able to establish itself as an industrial nation thanks to access to raw materials.

q225.why: Switzerland had no colonies. But Swiss companies bought and traded raw materials such as cotton from other countries' colonies and built up their industry in this way.

distractors.a: Switzerland never owned colonies of its own, even though Swiss companies and people were active in colonies.
distractors.b: There were Swiss mercenaries in foreign service, but this has nothing to do with the colonial period and industrialisation.

q226.question: Which founding cantons (Urkantone) formed an alliance in 1291?
q226.why: In 1291, the three valley communities on Lake Lucerne recorded their alliance in the Federal Charter (Bundesbrief). That is why they are called the founding cantons (Urkantone).

distractors.c: Zurich, Zug and Bern only joined the Confederation in the 14th century (1351 to 1353).
distractors.b: Geneva, Vaud and Fribourg were outside the alliance at that time; Geneva and Vaud only became cantons in the 19th century.

q227.question: Which people lived in the area of present-day Switzerland at the time of ancient Rome?
q227.why: The Helvetii were a Celtic people in the Plateau. The Romans conquered them after 58 BC, and Switzerland still bears their name today: Helvetia.

distractors.b: People only speak of Confederates (Eidgenossen) from the Middle Ages, more than 1000 years later.
distractors.c: The Etruscans lived in central Italy, not north of the Alps.

q228.question: Who fought against each other in the Sonderbund War of 1847?
q228.why: The Catholic conservative cantons of the Sonderbund fought against the liberal majority of the cantons. The Liberals won after about three weeks.

distractors.b: Zurich and Bern were both liberal and fought on the same side.
distractors.a: A fight between nobility and peasants fits the Middle Ages, not the Sonderbund War.

q229.question: From which ancient power and culture does the amphitheatre shown here (in Avenches) come?
q229.why: Amphitheatres with an arena and rows of seats are typical Roman buildings. At that time, Avenches was called Aventicum and was the Roman capital of the Helvetii.

distractors.a: The Gauls were Celts like the Helvetii; they did not build stone amphitheatres.
distractors.d: The Greeks built theatres, but not in Switzerland; the amphitheatre is a Roman type of building.

q230.question: In 1515, the Confederates lost the Battle of Marignano. What were the consequences of this defeat?

options.a: The Confederates gave up conquering further territories.
options.c: The peasants rose up against the governments in Bern, Zurich and Lucerne.
options.d: The Confederates attacked the city of Zurich.

q230.why: After the heavy defeat against France, the Confederates gave up Milan and concluded the «Perpetual Peace» in 1516. After that, the Confederation gave up its policy of conquest.

distractors.b: The Confederates kept their troops; Swiss mercenaries even continued to fight for France.
distractors.c: This describes the Peasants' War of 1653, not the consequences of Marignano.

q231.question: Which new religious denomination emerged with the Reformation?
q231.why: The reformers separated from the Catholic Church. This is how the Protestant churches came about, in Switzerland the Reformed Church.

distractors.a: Judaism is much older than Christianity and did not come from the Reformation.

q232.question: What led to the denominational split of Switzerland?
q232.why: With the Reformation, some cantons became Reformed and others stayed Catholic. As a result, there were two denominations in the Confederation.

distractors.a: The Anabaptists were a small group within the Reformation; they were persecuted, but did not split the country.
distractors.d: Monasteries were dissolved as a result of the Reformation; the cause of the split was the Reformation itself.
distractors.c: The general strike (Landesstreik) was in 1918 and had nothing to do with religion.

q233.question: What led to the political reorganisation of the Confederation in 1798?

options.d: the founding of the canton of Zurich

q233.why: French troops invaded in 1798 and defeated Bern. The Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed, and France set up the Helvetic Republic.

distractors.b: There was a revolution against Bern in Vaud in 1798, but the invasion by the French was decisive for the reorganisation.
distractors.d: Zurich had already been part of the Confederation since 1351.

q234.question: What did the European powers establish for Switzerland at the Congress of Vienna in 1815?

options.b: the abolition of customs duties at the Swiss borders

q234.why: After Napoleon, the great powers wanted a neutral zone in the middle of Europe. At the Congress of Vienna they established neutrality, and on 20 November 1815 they confirmed Switzerland's «perpetual neutrality».

distractors.c: Swiss mercenaries served in foreign armies for a long time after that; mercenary service was only banned in 1859.
distractors.d: Switzerland was not part of Austria; there was nothing it had to separate from in 1815.

q235.question: How was the Confederation redefined in the Federal Constitution of 1848?
q235.why: The Constitution of 1848 created a common federation but left the cantons a lot of their own power. That is a federalist federal state.

distractors.c: A centralised state existed only briefly, from 1798 to 1803; it was very unpopular.
distractors.d: Switzerland has no king; it is a republic.

q236.question: Which important humanitarian organisation was founded in Geneva in 1863?

options.c: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)

q236.why: Henry Dunant and other people from Geneva founded the ICRC in 1863 to help wounded soldiers in war.

distractors.a: Amnesty International was only founded in 1961 in London.
distractors.b: Pro Juventute is a Swiss foundation for children and young people, founded in 1912.
distractors.d: Swiss Solidarity (Glückskette) is a Swiss fundraising campaign for donations, founded in 1946.

q237.question: Which invention fundamentally changed Swiss industry in the 18th century?
q237.why: The steam engine could drive machines in factories. James Watt improved it in England in the 18th century. It made industrialisation possible, also in Switzerland.

distractors.a: Nikolaus Otto only built the Otto engine in 1876, so in the 19th century. At first it ran on gas, only later on petrol.
distractors.c: Electric motors only became important in factories in the late 19th century.

q237.note: Exam answer: «die Dampfmaschine» (the steam engine). Today: the study brochures say that industrialisation began in the 19th century with the steam engine. At first, Swiss factories mostly ran on water power; steam engines were only built in Switzerland from 1836 (HLS, «Dampfmaschine»).

q238.question: In 1877, child labour was banned in Switzerland. Why?

options.a: Children had to help at home on the farms.
options.b: Children could not be used for heavy and dangerous work anyway.
options.c: Children could not go to school because they worked in factories.
options.d: Children were hired out for work. But they earned too little there.

q238.why: Children worked many hours in factories and therefore could not go to school. The Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14.

distractors.a: The law only concerned factories; helping on the farm was not banned.
distractors.d: The reason for the ban was the children's health and education, not their low wages.

q239.question: Which insurance was introduced in Switzerland in 1948?
q239.why: The people approved the AHV in 1947, and from 1 January 1948 it paid the first pensions. This fulfilled an old demand of the national general strike of 1918.

distractors.b: Fire insurance for buildings had existed in many cantons long before.
distractors.d: Life insurance is private insurance and already existed in the 19th century.

q240.question: Since when have Swiss women been allowed to vote and elect at federal level?
q240.why: The men accepted women's suffrage on 7 February 1971. Since then, Swiss women citizens have been allowed to vote and elect at federal level.

distractors.c: In 1919, elections were held for the first time using proportional representation; but women were still not allowed to vote.
distractors.b: In 1946 there was still no women's suffrage; a popular vote in 1959 even failed.

q241.question: Who was the first woman on the Swiss Federal Council?
q241.why: On 2 October 1984, Parliament elected Elisabeth Kopp (FDP, Zurich) as the first woman to the Federal Council.

distractors.a: In 1993, Ruth Dreifuss was the second woman Federal Councillor, and in 1999 the first woman President of the Confederation.
distractors.c: Ruth Metzler was only elected in 1999.
distractors.d: Micheline Calmy-Rey was only elected in 2002.

q242.question: What laid the foundations of Switzerland's current relations with the EU?

options.a: the voters' approval of the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000
options.b: the rejection of EEA membership in the popular vote of 1992
options.c: the withdrawal of Switzerland's application for EU membership in 2016
options.d: Switzerland's accession to the UN in 2002

q242.why: The bilateral path began with the yes to the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000. It still governs the relationship with the EU today.

distractors.b: The no to the EEA in 1992 was the reason to look for another path. But the foundation itself is the Bilateral Agreements I.
distractors.c: Withdrawing the old membership application in 2016 was only a formal step. Relations were already governed by treaties before that.
distractors.d: Joining the UN has nothing to do with the EU.

q243.question: Who was William Tell?

options.a: a Swiss mercenary in foreign service
options.b: a legendary figure from Central Switzerland who fought against foreign rulers
options.c: a noble landlord in the Swiss Plateau
options.d: a leader in the Peasants' War

q243.why: Tell is a legendary figure from Central Switzerland. The story of the apple shot and the fight against the bailiff Gessler is not historically proven.

distractors.a: There were many mercenaries, but in the legend Tell fights for his homeland, not for money in foreign service.
distractors.d: The Peasants' War was in 1653, long after the Tell legend, which takes place in the 13th/14th century.

q244.question: Which organisation did Henry Dunant (1828-1910) found in Geneva?

options.c: the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)

q244.why: In 1859, Henry Dunant saw the suffering of wounded soldiers at Solferino. So in 1863 he and others founded the ICRC in Geneva.

distractors.a: Dunant did co-found the YMCA in Geneva in 1852. But the question means his best-known foundation, the ICRC (1863). In the test only c counts.
distractors.b: Pro Juventute was only founded in 1912, without Dunant.
distractors.d: The Universal Postal Union was founded in Bern in 1874, by states and not by Dunant.

q245.question: In which economic sector has Switzerland been a world leader for centuries?
q245.why: Swiss watches have been famous for their quality for centuries. They are still among Switzerland's most important exports today.

distractors.a: The textile industry used to be important in Eastern Switzerland, but today it is small and not a world leader.
distractors.c: Switzerland has no large car factories.

q246.question: Why did many Swiss people emigrate in the 19th century?

options.a: Because they were politically persecuted in Switzerland.
options.b: Because they wanted to gain professional experience.
options.c: Because hunger, poverty and unemployment prevailed.
options.d: Because they were looking for adventure.

q246.why: Crop failures, famines and a lack of work made many people poor. They looked for a better life in America.

distractors.a: There were few political refugees; most emigrants left because of economic hardship.
distractors.d: For some it was an adventure, but the main reason for the big waves of emigration was poverty.

q247.question: What was the Sechseläutenplatz used for during the Second World War?
q247.why: During the Second World War there was not enough food. In the «Anbauschlacht» (cultivation battle), potatoes were planted on the Sechseläutenplatz.

state_names.title: Names of Switzerland: Confederation, Confoederatio Helvetica, CH
intro: Switzerland has several names. The official name in the Federal Constitution is «Swiss Confederation» (Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft). In everyday life people often just say «Confederation» (Eidgenossenschaft). In Switzerland the word means roughly «state». It comes from «Eid», an oath, which is a solemn promise. In the Middle Ages the first places promised each other mutual help. Anyone who made such an alliance was a «Confederate» (Eidgenosse).

Switzerland has four national languages. So that no language is favoured, a Latin name is often used: «Confoederatio Helvetica». Confoederatio means alliance or confederation. The Helvetii were a Celtic people who lived here about 2000 years ago. Since the founding of the federal state in 1848, this has been the official Latin name. It appears, for example, on the 5-franc coin.

The abbreviation CH comes from Confoederatio Helvetica. You see it every day: on car number plates, in the internet address «.ch» and in the currency CHF, the Swiss franc. So if you understand the abbreviation, you also know the Latin name of the country. The authorities like to use it too.

key_terms.definition: Confederation: another name for Switzerland; originally an alliance of places that promised each other help with an oath.
Confoederatio Helvetica: the Latin name of Switzerland, meaning «Helvetic Confederation».
CH: abbreviation for Confoederatio Helvetica, for example on cars and in «.ch».

state_names.mnemonic: CH as in CHF (Swiss franc) and «.ch»: always Confoederatio Helvetica.

national_symbols.title: Flag, anthem and Helvetia
intro: The Swiss flag is red with a white cross in the middle. The arms of the cross are the same length and do not touch the edge. The shape is special: the national flag is square. Only a few countries have a square flag.

The flag is easy to confuse with others. The Red Cross is the reverse: a red cross on a white background. The emblem honours Switzerland. Henry Dunant, the founder of the Red Cross, was Swiss. The flag of Denmark is rectangular, and its cross is shifted to one side. The coat of arms of the canton of Schwyz is completely red with a small white cross in the upper corner.

The national anthem is called the «Swiss Psalm» (Schweizerpsalm). A psalm is a religious song. The song was written in 1841. Since 1981 it has officially been Switzerland's anthem. The text exists in all four national languages. You hear the anthem, for example, on 1 August, at official celebrations and at sports events when Swiss athletes win.

Helvetia is an invented female figure. She is an image that stands for the whole of Switzerland. This is called an allegory. Helvetia carries a spear and a shield with the Swiss cross. She can be seen on the 50-centime, 1-franc and 2-franc coins.

key_terms.definition: Swiss Psalm: the national anthem of Switzerland, official since 1981.
Helvetia: an invented female figure who represents Switzerland; she is shown on coins.
Allegory: a figure or image that stands for an idea or a country.

national_symbols.mnemonic: Swiss flag: white cross on red, square. Red Cross: exactly the reverse.

national_day.title: 1 August
intro: Switzerland's National Day is on 1 August. It commemorates the Federal Charter of 1291. At that time Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other mutual help. This story is seen as the beginning of the Confederation. On 1 August there are speeches, fireworks and bonfires on the hills, and many houses are decorated with flags.

1 August is the only public holiday that the Confederation sets for the whole of Switzerland. This is written in the Federal Constitution. Since 1994 the day has been a day off work everywhere. The cantons regulate other public holidays such as Ascension Day, Good Friday or 1 May. That is why they are not the same in all cantons.

Do not confuse 1 August with the national days of other countries. France celebrates on 14 July, the USA on 4 July and Germany on 3 October. 1 May is Labour Day, and in some cantons it is a full or half day off. But it is not a Swiss National Day.

key_terms.definition: Federal holiday: 1 August, Switzerland's National Day, set in the Federal Constitution.
Federal Charter: a document from 1291 in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help.

national_day.mnemonic: 1291 and 1 August: on the first day of August, Switzerland celebrates its first alliance.

regions.title: Jura, Plateau, Alps
intro: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe and has no access to the sea. Such a country is called a landlocked country. Goods from overseas therefore come via ports in other countries or by ship up the Rhine to Basel. Switzerland is also not an island and not an exclave, which means it is not a separated piece of another country.

Switzerland has three large regions. In the north-west is the Jura, a mountain range with long, low ridges. In the south and east are the Alps with high mountains. In between lies the Plateau (Mittelland), an area with hills, lakes and rivers. The Alps cover about 60 percent of the area, the Plateau about 30 percent and the Jura about 10 percent.

About two thirds of the population live in the Plateau. There the land is flat enough for towns, industry, roads and agriculture. Large cities such as Zurich, Bern and Lausanne are located there. Far fewer people live in the Alps, although they make up the largest part of the country.

key_terms.definition: Landlocked country: a country without access to the sea.
Plateau: the flatter area between the Jura and the Alps, where most people live.
Jura: a mountain range in north-western Switzerland, along the border with France.

regions.mnemonic: From north-west to south-east: Jura, Plateau, Alps. The Plateau is in the middle, and that is where most people live.

mountains.title: Mountains and passes
intro: The Alps shape Switzerland. Passes lead over the mountains. A pass is the lowest point where you can cross a mountain range. Well-known Alpine passes are the Gotthard, the Simplon and the Great St Bernard. For centuries they have connected the north with Italy. Today important roads and tunnels also run through there.

Cantons with many high mountains are called mountain cantons. Examples are Valais, Graubünden, Uri and Ticino. Valais has the most four-thousand-metre peaks in Switzerland. Cantons such as Zurich, Aargau or Schaffhausen, on the other hand, lie in the Plateau or on the Rhine and have no high mountains.

The highest point in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze in Valais, 4634 metres high. It belongs to the Monte Rosa massif on the border with Italy. But the most famous mountain is the Matterhorn near Zermatt with its pointed pyramid shape. It is 4478 metres high and can be seen on many pictures and packages.

key_terms.definition: Alpine pass: a crossing over the Alps, for example the Gotthard or the Simplon.
Mountain canton: a canton that lies mostly in the mountains, for example Valais.
Dufourspitze: the highest mountain in Switzerland (4634 m), in Valais.

mountains.mnemonic: The Matterhorn is the best-known mountain, the Dufourspitze the highest.

rivers.title: Rhine and Rhone
intro: Large European rivers have their source in the Swiss Alps. That is why Switzerland is also called the water tower of Europe. The water from Switzerland flows into different seas. More than 5 percent of Europe's drinking water reserves are in Switzerland. Switzerland uses the water of its rivers and lakes to produce a lot of electricity in hydroelectric power stations.

The Rhine has its source in Graubünden. It flows through Lake Constance, then to Basel and on through Germany and the Netherlands. There it flows into the North Sea. From Basel onwards the Rhine is navigable. The Rhine ports are important for Switzerland's trade.

The Rhone has its source at the Rhone Glacier in Valais. It flows through Lake Geneva and then south through France. It flows into the Mediterranean. Other rivers take other routes: the Inn from the Engadine flows via the Danube into the Black Sea, the Ticino via the Po into the Adriatic.

key_terms.definition: Rhine: a river from Graubünden that flows via Basel into the North Sea.
Rhone: a river from Valais that flows through Lake Geneva into the Mediterranean.

rivers.mnemonic: Rhine to the north into the North Sea, Rhone to the south into the Mediterranean.

climate.title: Föhn, climate change and spatial planning
intro: Switzerland has typical winds. The Föhn is a warm and dry wind from the south. The air rises on the south side of the Alps and loses its rain there. On the north side it drops down into the valley and becomes warm. The Bise, on the other hand, is a cold wind from the north-east.

Climate change is clearly noticeable in Switzerland. Temperatures are rising, also in the mountains. That is why the glaciers are melting and getting smaller every year. The forest also suffers from heat and drought. Spruces, for example, need a lot of water. Foresters therefore plant other tree species that tolerate warmth better, for example oaks.

Switzerland is small, and many people want to build. Spatial planning regulates where you may build and where you may not. There are building zones and areas outside the building zones. This protects agricultural land and undeveloped landscapes. The goal is also described as: preventing urban sprawl.

key_terms.definition: Föhn: a warm, dry downslope wind, in Switzerland mostly from the south.
Bise: a cold, dry wind from the north-east.
Spatial planning: planning how land is used, where building takes place and which landscapes remain free.
Urban sprawl: when houses are built scattered across the open countryside.

climate.mnemonic: Föhn like the hair dryer (German: Föhn): warm and dry.

neighbours.title: Neighbouring countries
intro: Switzerland borders on five countries. To the north is Germany. To the east are Austria and Liechtenstein. To the south is Italy. To the west is France. Switzerland does not reach the sea anywhere. Spain, Portugal or Croatia are in Europe, but they are not direct neighbours of Switzerland. There are always other countries between them and Switzerland.

The neighbours also explain the languages. On the border with France, people speak French. On the border with Italy, in Ticino and in parts of Graubünden, people speak Italian. In the north and east people speak German, as in Germany and Austria. Liechtenstein is a small country between Switzerland and Austria. It uses the Swiss franc.

key_terms.definition: Neighbouring countries: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

neighbours.mnemonic: Clockwise from the north: Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein, Italy, France.

size.title: Extent and largest cantons
intro: Switzerland is a small country. Its area is just over 41'000 square kilometres. From north to south it measures about 220 kilometres. From west to east it is longer, about 350 kilometres. By car you can cross the country in a few hours, unless mountains are in the way.

The 26 cantons vary greatly in size. The largest canton is Graubünden in the east. It is a mountain canton and covers about one sixth of Switzerland. But only about 200'000 people live there. The smallest canton is Basel-Stadt. Zurich has the most inhabitants, but it is not the largest canton by area.

key_terms.definition: Extent: the greatest length of a country in one direction, for example from north to south.
Graubünden: the largest canton of Switzerland by area.

size.mnemonic: Switzerland lies sideways: about 350 km wide, but only 220 km high.

cities.title: Bern, Zurich and the large cities
intro: The largest city in Switzerland is Zurich. About 450'000 people live there. It is followed by Geneva, Basel, Lausanne and Bern. Zurich is the most important centre for business and banks. The large cities all lie in the Plateau. Basel is on the Rhine on the border with Germany and France, Geneva on Lake Geneva.

Bern is not the largest city, but it is the city of the government. The Federal Council and Parliament work there in the Federal Palace. That is why Bern is considered the capital of Switzerland. Officially Bern is called the «federal city» (Bundesstadt). International organisations have their seat elsewhere: the UN has its European seat in Geneva, FIFA is in Zurich. The Council of Europe is in Strasbourg in France.

Among the cantons, too, Zurich is number one. More than 1.5 million people live in the canton of Zurich (end of 2025: about 1.63 million). That is almost one in five people in Switzerland. It is followed by the cantons of Bern and Vaud. The fewest people live in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, only about 16'000.

key_terms.definition: Federal city: the official term for Bern as the seat of government and Parliament.
Federal Palace: the building in Bern where the Federal Council and Parliament work.

cities.mnemonic: Zurich is the largest, Bern governs.

population.title: Population and share of foreigners
intro: Today just over 9 million people live in Switzerland. The test often uses older figures «as of 2020». At that time there were about 8.6 million. Learn this figure for the test. The population is growing mainly because people immigrate from other countries.

About a quarter of the population does not have a Swiss passport. In 2020 that was about 2.1 million people, or about 25 percent. Today the share is somewhat higher, almost 28 percent. Many foreigners were born in Switzerland or have lived here for a long time.

Most foreigners come from Europe. About two thirds come from an EU or EFTA country. The largest groups come from Italy, Germany, Portugal and France. The free movement of persons with the EU makes it easier to work and live in Switzerland.

key_terms.definition: Permanent resident population: all people who live permanently in Switzerland, with and without a Swiss passport.
Share of foreigners: the part of the population without a Swiss passport, in percent.
Free movement of persons: an agreement that allows people from the EU to live and work in Switzerland, and the other way round.

population.mnemonic: As of 2020: 8.6 million people, of whom 2.1 million foreigners, so a quarter. Two thirds of them from the EU.

national_languages.title: German, French, Italian, Romansh
intro: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. This is written in the Federal Constitution. English is not a national language, even though many people speak it at work. Portuguese or Spanish are not national languages either, although many immigrants speak them.

The fourth national language is Romansh. It comes from Latin and is spoken only in Graubünden. Less than one percent of the population speaks it. Romansh has been a national language since 1938. The aim was to protect this small language. Romansh has several regional forms, for example in the Engadine.

Most people speak German, almost two thirds. In everyday life in German-speaking Switzerland people speak dialect, that is Swiss German. But they write in standard German. The dialects do not count as separate national languages. Just over one fifth speak French, about 8 percent Italian. In addition, there are many other languages spoken by immigrants.

key_terms.definition: National language: one of the four languages that the Federal Constitution names as languages of Switzerland.
Romansh: the smallest national language, spoken in Graubünden.

national_languages.mnemonic: Four languages: G, F, I and R (German, French, Italian, Romansh).

language_regions.title: Language regions and the Röstigraben
intro: Each national language has its region. German-speaking Switzerland is in the north, the centre and the east. French-speaking Switzerland in the west is called Romandie or Welschland. In Ticino and in some southern valleys of Graubünden people speak Italian. Romansh is spoken only in parts of Graubünden.

Some cantons have more than one official language. Fribourg, Bern and Valais are bilingual: German and French. In the city of Fribourg the language border runs right through the city. Graubünden is even trilingual: German, Romansh and Italian. Ticino is the only canton in which Italian alone is the official language.

Between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandie there are sometimes cultural differences, for example in popular votes. This invisible border is jokingly called the «Röstigraben» (rösti ditch). Rösti is a potato dish that is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. So the Röstigraben is not a real ditch but an image for these differences.

key_terms.definition: Romandie / Welschland: French-speaking Switzerland in the west.
Röstigraben (rösti ditch): an image for the cultural boundary between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandie.
Bilingual canton: a canton with two official languages, for example Fribourg, Bern or Valais.

language_regions.mnemonic: Rösti is eaten on this side of the ditch, croissants on the other side.

democracy.title: What is a democracy?
intro: Switzerland is a democracy. The word comes from Greek and means «rule of the people». In a democracy, power is not held by a king, a prince or a dictator. Power lies with the people. The opposite is, for example, a dictatorship, a principality or an absolutist state. There a single person or a small group decides, and the people have no say.

Elections are an important feature of democracy. The people elect a parliament. The elected politicians are the people's representatives. They make the laws in the name of the people. Elections take place regularly, at federal level every four years. In this way the people can decide again and again who should represent them. Anyone who does a bad job may not be re-elected.

Switzerland goes even further: it is a direct democracy. The people do not only elect, they also vote on specific issues. Travelling freely or a basic income, on the other hand, are not features of a democracy. They may or may not apply in a democracy. What matters is this: the people have a say.

key_terms.definition: Democracy: a form of state in which the people hold power and have a say.
People's representatives: the persons in parliament elected by the people, who decide for the people.
Dictatorship: a form of state in which one person or a small group rules alone.

democracy.mnemonic: «Demos» means people, «kratie» means rule: in a democracy the people rule.

rule_of_law.title: Rule of law and monopoly on the use of force
intro: Switzerland is a state governed by the rule of law. This means: the laws apply to everyone. They apply to Swiss citizens, to foreigners and also to politicians. They also apply to people who said no in a popular vote. And above all: the state, too, must abide by the laws. It may not act arbitrarily.

That is why the state may not arrest or imprison anyone without reason. This requires a reason in the law and a regulated procedure. In a state governed by the rule of law, however, you may criticise laws and question the work of the authorities. You may also join a religious group. This is protected by fundamental rights, for example freedom of opinion and freedom of religion.

Only the state may use force against people or property, for example the police or the military. This is called the monopoly on the use of force. Anyone who commits a criminal offence is punished according to the law. A court decides the punishment, not the victim. Vigilante justice, that is taking revenge on your own, is prohibited. Even people who report themselves are usually punished; however, the court can reduce the punishment.

key_terms.definition: State governed by the rule of law: a state in which the laws apply to everyone, including the state itself.
Monopoly on the use of force: only the state, for example the police and the military, may use force.
Vigilante justice: when someone takes revenge or punishes someone themselves instead of letting the police and the courts act. This is prohibited.
Criminal offence: an act that a law prohibits and that is punished, for example theft.

rule_of_law.mnemonic: Under the rule of law, the law stands above everyone, even above the state.

three_levels.title: Three levels of government and 26 cantons
intro: Switzerland is a federal state. Federalism means: power is distributed across several levels. Switzerland has three levels of government. The highest level is the Confederation, that is the whole of Switzerland. The middle level is the cantons. The lowest level is the municipalities. Each level has its own tasks, its own authorities and levies its own taxes.

The federal state is made up of 26 cantons. In the past people spoke of 20 cantons and 6 half-cantons. Examples of half-cantons are Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft. In popular votes they each have only half a cantonal vote. Other countries have similar units with other names: Germany and Austria have federal states (Länder), Italy and Canada have provinces. In Switzerland they are called cantons.

Each canton is divided into municipalities. In 2021 there were about 2200 political municipalities in Switzerland. Because municipalities keep merging, the number is falling. In some cantons, for example the canton of Zurich, there are also districts between the canton and the municipality. But the districts are not a separate level of government, only administrative areas of the canton.

key_terms.definition: Federalism: power in the state is distributed across several levels: Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
Confederation: the highest level of government, that is the Swiss state as a whole.
Canton: one of the 26 member states of Switzerland, for example Zurich or Bern.
Municipality: the lowest level of government, for example a town or a village.
Half-canton: former name for the 6 cantons with only half a cantonal vote, for example Basel-Stadt.

three_levels.mnemonic: From top to bottom: Confederation, canton, municipality. 26 cantons = 20 full + 6 half.

federal_tasks.title: Tasks of the Confederation
intro: In federalism each level has its own tasks. The Confederation only does what the Federal Constitution expressly allows it to do. These are mainly tasks that must be the same for the whole country. All other tasks belong to the cantons. The cantons pass some tasks on to the municipalities.

Important tasks of the Confederation are: foreign policy, that is relations with other states; the military and the internal and external security of the country; customs at the border; money and monetary policy; social security (for example the AHV); and the protection of the environment. The Swiss National Bank conducts monetary policy on behalf of the Confederation. It sets the key interest rates itself and independently.

The cantons and municipalities, on the other hand, are responsible for state schools, the police, hospitals, building regulations and the election of cantonal judges. The municipalities often take care of water supply, the fire service and parks. The Confederation does not produce cars, does not run its own hospitals and does not publish newspapers. Nor does it organise the work in companies.

key_terms.definition: Foreign policy: Switzerland's relations with other states and international organisations.
Monetary policy: control of the money supply and interest rates. It is the responsibility of the Confederation and the National Bank.
Customs: the control of goods and persons at the national border and the duties charged on them.
Social security: the social insurance schemes such as AHV and IV that protect people in old age, invalidity or unemployment.

federal_tasks.mnemonic: What happens at the border or applies to the whole country (army, customs, foreign policy, franc) is done by the Confederation. What happens on your doorstep (school, police, water, fire service) is done by the canton and the municipality.

separation_of_powers.title: Legislature, executive, judiciary (and the media)
intro: In Switzerland the power of the state is divided among three branches. This is called the separation of powers. In German the word «Gewalt» here does not mean violence but power. No person and no authority should have all the power. The branches control each other. This prevents abuse of power. The separation of powers exists at all three levels of government: in the Confederation, in the cantons and in the municipalities.

At federal level: the legislative power (legislature) lies with the Federal Parliament, made up of the National Council and the Council of States. It makes the laws. The executive power (executive) lies with the Federal Council, that is the government. It implements the laws. The judicial power (judiciary) lies with the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne. It decides disputes and judges according to the law.

The media, that is newspapers, radio, television and online media, are often called the «fourth power». They are not part of the state. But they inform the population and criticise politics and the authorities. In this way they also control power. The separation of powers does not mean the separation of state and church or the division of Parliament into two chambers.

key_terms.definition: Separation of powers: the power of the state is divided among parliament, government and the courts.
Legislature: the legislative power, at federal level the Parliament (National Council and Council of States).
Executive: the executive power, that is the government, at federal level the Federal Council.
Judiciary: the judicial power, that is the courts, at federal level the Federal Supreme Court.
Fourth power: the media, which observe politics and the authorities critically.

separation_of_powers.mnemonic: Legislature = make laws (legislate), executive = carry out (execute), judiciary = judge (judge).

justice_police.title: Courts and police
intro: Judges work at courts. Their task is to deliver judgments. They decide whether someone has broken a law and what punishment they receive. They also decide disputes between people or with authorities. They do not defend the accused; a lawyer does that. Nor do they write laws; Parliament does that.

The police ensure security and order. They prosecute violations of the law: they investigate criminal offences and look for the offenders. In principle, only the police may make arrests. A vigilante group or a municipal authority may not. Private persons may only hold an offender briefly in an emergency until the police arrive. But the police do not deliver judgments. The judgment is always given by a court. In this way the police and the courts remain separate.

The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne is the highest court in Switzerland. Its judges are elected by the United Federal Assembly, that is by the National Council and the Council of States together. There is no normal application process with a job interview. The Federal Council does not appoint judges and the cantons do not send their own representatives.

key_terms.definition: Court judgment: the decision of a court in a criminal case or dispute.
Federal Supreme Court: the highest court in Switzerland, based in Lausanne.
Violation of the law: a breach of a law.
Arrest: the police take a suspect into custody.

justice_police.mnemonic: The police catch, the court judges.

parliament_chambers.title: National Council and Council of States
intro: The Swiss Parliament is called the Federal Assembly. It has two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States. The National Council has 200 members. It represents the people. Large cantons have more seats than small ones. The Council of States has 46 members. It mainly represents the cantons. Each canton has two seats, the six former half-cantons one each. Together there are 246 members.

Both chambers are equally strong. Normally they meet separately. Sometimes they meet in a joint session. They are then called the United Federal Assembly. It consists of all members of the National Council and the Council of States. Parliament has its seat in the Federal Palace in Bern. The Federal Council also works there.

The members of Parliament are elected by the people, namely by the Swiss citizens who are entitled to vote. Foreigners may not vote at federal level. The parties put forward candidates, but it is the people who elect. The elections take place every four years, most recently in 2023, next in 2027.

key_terms.definition: Federal Assembly: the Swiss Parliament with the National Council and the Council of States.
National Council: the large chamber with 200 members. It represents the people.
Council of States: the small chamber with 46 members. It represents the cantons.
United Federal Assembly: the National Council and the Council of States in a joint session.
Federal Palace: the building in Bern where Parliament and the Federal Council work.

parliament_chambers.mnemonic: 200 + 46 = 246. «Stände» is an old word for cantons: the Council of States (Ständerat) represents the cantons.

parliament_tasks.title: What Parliament does
intro: The most important task of the Federal Assembly is legislation. The National Council and the Council of States debate and pass the federal laws. Both chambers must approve a law. In this way Parliament decides on most new laws. The Federal Council proposes laws, but it does not pass them. The Federal Supreme Court applies laws, but it does not make them.

The people often have the last word. A referendum can be called against a new law. This requires 50 000 signatures. Then the people vote on the law. That is why people say: the National Council, the Council of States and the people decide on laws. Elections and popular votes, on the other hand, are organised by the Federal Council, the Federal Chancellery and the cantons.

Parliament has other tasks too. It adopts the federal budget, which the Federal Council prepares. It approves international treaties and supervises the government. As the United Federal Assembly, that is in a joint session, the National Council and the Council of States elect the seven members of the Federal Council, the Federal Chancellor and the judges of the Federal Supreme Court.

key_terms.definition: Legislation: debating and passing laws. At federal level this is the main task of Parliament.
Referendum: the right of the people to vote on a law passed by Parliament.
Budget: the plan for the Confederation's income and expenditure for one year.

parliament_tasks.mnemonic: Parliament makes laws. Together it elects the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.

federal_council.title: Federal Council and the principle of collegiality
intro: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It holds executive power (the executive) at federal level. It runs the government business: it implements the laws, plans policy and represents Switzerland in relation to other states. In the cantons the government has a different name, for example Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat). In some cantons the Grand Council or the Landrat is the cantonal parliament.

The Federal Council has seven members. The people do not elect them directly. The United Federal Assembly, that is the National Council and the Council of States together, elects them for four years. Each year one member is President of the Confederation. But this person does not have more power than the others.

The principle of collegiality applies in the Federal Council. The seven members decide together as a body. They try to reach agreement; if necessary, they vote. In public, all members must represent the decision in the same way, even if they personally or their party have a different opinion. In this way the Federal Council speaks with one voice.

key_terms.definition: Federal Council: the government of Switzerland with seven members.
Principle of collegiality: the Federal Council decides together, and all members represent the decision in the same way in public.
President of the Confederation: a member of the Federal Council who chairs the meetings and represents Switzerland for one year.

federal_council.mnemonic: Seven heads, one voice: that is the principle of collegiality.

administration.title: Departments and the Federal Chancellery
intro: The Federal Council needs many employees to do its work. They work in the Federal Administration. It is divided into seven departments, one for each member of the Federal Council. A department is similar to a ministry in other countries. Each Federal Councillor heads a department.

The seven departments are: the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA, German: EDA), the Federal Department of Home Affairs (FDHA, German: EDI), the Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP, German: EJPD), the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS, German: VBS), the Federal Department of Finance (FDF, German: EFD), the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research (EAER, German: WBF) and the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC, German: UVEK). There is no separate department just for food, climate or schools.

In addition, there is the Federal Chancellery. It is the staff office of the Federal Council. It is headed by the Federal Chancellor, since 2024 Viktor Rossi. The Federal Chancellery supports the Federal Council, prepares its meetings and helps organise federal elections and popular votes. The Federal Chancellor is not a member of the Federal Council. He does not govern, does not elect anyone and does not make laws.

key_terms.definition: Federal Administration: all the offices and employees who work for the Federal Council.
Department: one of the seven large areas of the Federal Administration, headed by a member of the Federal Council.
Federal Chancellery: the staff office that supports the Federal Council in its work.
Federal Chancellor: the person who heads the Federal Chancellery and supports the Federal Council.

administration.mnemonic: Seven Federal Councillors, seven departments. Unlike in Germany, the Chancellor in Switzerland does not govern, but only supports.

voting_rights.title: Who may vote in elections and popular votes?
intro: At federal level, only people who have Swiss citizenship and are at least 18 years old may have a say. These people are called voters (Stimmberechtigte). Where you were born, how much tax you pay or whether you have a criminal record does not matter. Only a few adults are excluded: those who permanently cannot decide for themselves because of a serious mental illness or disability.

There are two sides. The right to vote (active suffrage) means: I may vote in elections and popular votes. The right to stand for election (passive suffrage) means: I can be elected myself, for example to the National Council. At federal level, every person entitled to vote can be elected. You do not need a particular job for this, and you do not have to speak several national languages.

Foreigners may never take part in national elections and popular votes, not even with a C settlement permit. You only get this right through naturalisation. Foreigners have other rights before that, for example joining an association or choosing their job. Some cantons and municipalities, mainly in western Switzerland, allow foreigners to vote at their level. This does not exist in the canton of Zurich.

key_terms.definition: Voters: Swiss citizens aged 18 and over who may vote in elections and popular votes.
Right to vote (active suffrage): the right to vote yourself in elections and popular votes.
Right to stand for election (passive suffrage): the right to be elected to political office.
Naturalisation: foreigners receive Swiss citizenship and with it all political rights.

voting_rights.mnemonic: Active: I elect. Passive: I am elected.

swiss_abroad.title: Swiss citizens abroad
intro: More than 800'000 Swiss citizens live abroad. They are called Swiss abroad or the «Fifth Switzerland». They keep their citizenship and their political rights. They may take part in national popular votes and elections, even if they have not lived in Switzerland for many years.

To do this, they register with the Swiss representation in their country of residence, that is the embassy or the consulate. They are then entered in the electoral register of a Swiss municipality. The voting documents are sent abroad by post. You fill them in and send them back to the municipality. In some cantons e-voting, that is electronic voting, is also possible.

Nobody has to travel to Switzerland to do this. Swiss abroad may also be politically active in their country of residence, as far as the law there allows. Each canton decides for itself whether they may also take part in cantonal votes. Swiss abroad may also sign popular initiatives and referendums.

key_terms.definition: Swiss abroad: Swiss citizens who live abroad.
Fifth Switzerland: another name for all Swiss citizens living abroad.
Electoral register: a municipality's list of all the people who may vote there.

voting_practice.title: How and when people vote
intro: At federal level there are normally four voting dates per year. These dates are reserved many years in advance. If you add the canton and the municipality, people vote about four to five times a year. On one date people often vote on several proposals at the same time. Cantons and municipalities usually put their own votes on the same days.

Popular votes and elections always take place on a Sunday. On that day the polling station, the ballot box, is open in the morning. By Sunday evening the results are already known. The elections to the National Council take place every four years in October, also on a Sunday.

But most voters do not go to the ballot box at all. They vote by post. About three to four weeks before the date, the documents arrive at home. You fill in the ballot paper and send it back or put it in the municipality's letterbox. E-voting exists only as a trial in a few cantons. You cannot vote by telephone.

key_terms.definition: Ballot box: the place or the box where you hand in your ballot paper in person.
Postal voting: you send the completed ballot paper to the municipality by post.
Proposal: the topic or law that you vote on.

voting_practice.mnemonic: Four times a year, always on a Sunday, mostly by post.

referendum.title: The referendum: stopping a law
intro: Parliament makes the laws. The National Council and the Council of States pass them together. But the people can stop a new law. The tool for this is called a referendum. In a referendum the people say yes or no to a decision that Parliament has already made.

There are two types. The optional referendum is voluntary. Anyone who is against a new federal law collects 50'000 signatures within 100 days. Then there is a popular vote, and a majority of the people is enough. Eight cantons together can also demand a referendum. If there are no signatures, the law simply comes into force.

The mandatory referendum happens automatically, without signatures. This applies to every amendment of the Federal Constitution and to joining certain international organisations, for example the EU or NATO. Here a double majority is needed. There is no referendum against decisions of the Federal Council, the administration or the courts.

key_terms.definition: Referendum: the people vote on a decision of Parliament and can stop it in this way.
Optional referendum: voluntary; 50'000 signatures in 100 days against a new law.
Mandatory referendum: an automatic popular vote, for example on every amendment of the Federal Constitution.

referendum.mnemonic: Referendum = react: you fight back against something Parliament has already decided. 50'000 signatures in 100 days.

initiative.title: The popular initiative: amending the Constitution
intro: With a popular initiative, the people themselves bring in a new idea. A group of citizens proposes an amendment to the Federal Constitution. In this way important concerns of the population come to a vote, even if the government and Parliament do not want them. That is why the initiative is an important political right.

First a committee collects signatures. It needs 100'000 valid signatures within 18 months. All voters may sign, including Swiss abroad. Then Parliament debates the initiative and gives a recommendation. It can also make a counter-proposal. Finally, the people and the cantons vote on it.

At federal level an initiative always amends the Federal Constitution, not a law directly. It cannot remove Parliament from office and cannot replace the Federal Council. It may also not violate mandatory international law, for example the prohibition of torture. An initiative is only accepted if the people and the cantons say yes.

key_terms.definition: Popular initiative: a proposal from the people to amend the Federal Constitution.
Collection of signatures: a popular initiative needs 100'000 valid signatures in 18 months.
Counter-proposal: Parliament's own solution, which it puts forward against the initiative.

initiative.mnemonic: Initiative = idea, something new: 100'000 signatures in 18 months. Referendum = stop: 50'000 in 100 days.

double_majority.title: Majority of the people and majority of the cantons
intro: In some popular votes it is not enough for more than half of the voters to say yes. A majority of the cantons is also needed. This is called the double majority: majority of the people and majority of the cantons.

The majority of the people counts all votes in the whole of Switzerland. For the majority of the cantons, you count how each canton voted. The result in the canton is its cantonal vote. The 20 cantons each have one full vote, the 6 former half-cantons (for example Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft) each have half a vote. That makes 23 votes.

The double majority is needed for popular initiatives and for all amendments of the Federal Constitution. If one of the two majorities is missing, the proposal is rejected. For an optional referendum against a law, on the other hand, the majority of the people is enough. In this way the cantons with a large population cannot simply outvote the small cantons on the Constitution.

key_terms.definition: Majority of the people: more than half of all valid votes in the whole of Switzerland say yes.
Majority of the cantons: the majority of cantons votes yes.
Double majority: majority of the people and majority of the cantons together, needed for initiatives and constitutional amendments.

double_majority.mnemonic: «Stände» is an old word for cantons. That is also why the Council of States is called Ständerat.

direct_democracy.title: Direct democracy at a glance
intro: Switzerland is a semi-direct democracy. The people elect Parliament, and Parliament makes the laws. But in addition, the people also decide directly on specific issues. There are popular votes several times a year. This is rare worldwide. In many other countries the people only elect the parliament and do not decide on laws themselves. This is called indirect democracy.

There are two important tools for this. With the popular initiative, the people bring in a new idea for the Constitution. With the referendum, they vote on decisions of Parliament, for example on a new law. In this way the voters have a direct influence on the Constitution and the laws.

Not everything is put to the people. There are no votes on party programmes, radio and television programme schedules or filling posts in the administration. The Federal Council is not elected by the people but by the Federal Assembly. Taking part in a party is an indirect way of influencing politics.

key_terms.definition: Direct democracy: the people themselves decide on specific issues, not only on people.
Semi-direct democracy: a mix of a parliament that makes laws and people's rights such as the initiative and the referendum.
People's rights: the political rights of the people, above all the initiative and the referendum.

parties.title: Parties
intro: A political party is an association of people with similar political goals. They join together to reach these goals together. Parties deal, for example, with the economy, social issues or the environment. Anyone can join a party. You do not have to be a member of parliament to do so.

Parties represent the various interests and concerns of the population. They put forward candidates for elections. Before popular votes they give recommendations. They also often call referendums or launch initiatives. In this way they help people to form an opinion.

There are many parties in Switzerland, for example the SVP, SP, FDP, The Centre (Die Mitte), the Greens and the Green Liberals. No party has a majority on its own. Parties do not elect the government themselves: the Federal Council is elected by the Federal Assembly. Nor do they control the media, because the media are free.

key_terms.definition: Party: an association of people with similar political goals.
Voting recommendation: a party's advice to vote yes or no on a proposal.

interest_groups.title: Trade unions, associations, NGOs
intro: Besides the parties there are many organisations that stand up for certain groups or topics. They are called associations or interest groups. They talk to the authorities, give their opinion on new laws and take part in voting campaigns. They are an important part of Swiss politics.

Trade unions represent employees. They campaign, for example, for fair wages and good working conditions. Examples are Unia and the Swiss Trade Union Federation. On the other side are the employers' associations. Economiesuisse is the umbrella organisation of the Swiss economy and represents companies. For small businesses and crafts there is the Swiss Trade Association (Gewerbeverband).

There are also non-governmental organisations, NGOs for short. They work independently of the state. Amnesty International campaigns worldwide for respect for human rights, for example against torture and the death penalty. Other NGOs deal with the environment, climate, biodiversity or animal welfare, for example WWF or Pro Natura.

key_terms.definition: Trade union: an association that represents the interests of employees.
Employees: people who are employed by an employer and receive a wage.
Economiesuisse: the umbrella organisation of the Swiss economy; it represents companies.
NGO: a non-governmental organisation, that is an organisation independent of the state.

interest_groups.mnemonic: Trade union = for those who work. Economiesuisse = «economy»: for companies.

media.title: Newspapers and editorial teams
intro: In Switzerland there is freedom of the media. It is in the Federal Constitution, and censorship is prohibited. The state may not decide what appears in a newspaper, on the radio or on television. Free media are important for democracy. For example, they inform people about popular votes and they keep a check on those in power.

The editorial team decides what appears in a newspaper. The editorial team is the group of journalists at a newspaper. There is no media police and no state office that chooses the articles. But journalists must obey the laws, for example on the protection of privacy.

There are daily newspapers and weekly newspapers. Daily newspapers appear almost every day, for example the Tages-Anzeiger, the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ) or Blick. Weekly newspapers appear only once a week. One example is the SonntagsZeitung: it appears every Sunday, so once a week.

key_terms.definition: Editorial team: the team at a newspaper that decides which articles appear.
