Freedom of the media: newspapers, radio and television may report freely, without censorship by the state.
Weekly newspaper: a newspaper that appears once a week.

media.mnemonic: The name gives it away: the «Sonntags» (Sunday) Zeitung only comes out on Sunday, so once a week.

freedoms.title: Freedom of opinion, freedom of religion and the right to property
intro: Fundamental rights are rights that every person has in relation to the state. They are in the Federal Constitution. The state must respect and protect them. It may only restrict them if there is a law and an important public reason for it. Most fundamental rights apply to all people in Switzerland, including foreigners. Without them, nobody could hold their own political opinion without fear.

Important fundamental rights are freedom of expression and information: I may say what I think and get information freely. Freedom of religion and conscience is also called religious freedom: I may freely choose and practise my religion, or have none. There is also freedom of assembly and the guarantee of property. The guarantee of property protects personal property.

Many wishes are not fundamental rights. There is no fundamental right to a home, a job, the internet, Wi-Fi, television or pets. Owning weapons is not a fundamental right either; it is strictly regulated in the Weapons Act. But this is guaranteed: compulsory school is free of charge. And anyone in need has a right to help for the bare necessities.

key_terms.definition: Fundamental right: a right that every person has in relation to the state, set out in the Federal Constitution.
Freedom of expression and information: every person may say what they think and get information freely.
Freedom of religion and conscience: every person may freely choose and practise their religion, or have none.
Guarantee of property: personal property is protected against the state.

equality.title: Equality before the law and prohibition of discrimination
intro: Equality before the law means: all people are equal before the law. The same rules apply to everyone, whether rich or poor, Swiss or foreign. But this does not mean that everyone earns the same amount or has the same amount of holiday. The cantons may also have different laws.

Women and men have equal rights. In principle, they have the same rights and obligations in the family, at work and in politics. They have a right to equal pay for work of equal value. Cooking or bringing up children is not the business of one sex only. But there is no fixed quota for political bodies.

The prohibition of discrimination protects people against unfair treatment. Nobody may be treated worse because of their origin, skin colour, sex, age, language, religion, disability or way of life. For example, anyone who does not get a job or is not allowed into the swimming pool because of their skin colour is being discriminated against. The prohibition of discrimination is part of equality before the law and is also in the Federal Constitution.

key_terms.definition: Equality before the law: all people are equal before the law.
Equal rights: women and men have the same rights.
Discrimination: someone is treated worse because of a characteristic such as skin colour or sex.
Prohibition of discrimination: the fundamental right that forbids such unfair treatment.

laws_codes.title: Federal Constitution, ZGB, OR, StGB
intro: The constitution of Switzerland is called the Federal Constitution, abbreviated BV. It is the highest law of the country. It contains the fundamental rights and sets out how the state works. The first Federal Constitution dates from 1848; the current one has been in force since 2000. It is sometimes also called Switzerland's Basic Law, but its official name is Federal Constitution.

Below the Constitution there are many laws. The Civil Code (ZGB) governs how people live together: marriage and divorce, family, children, inheritance and property. The Code of Obligations (OR) governs contracts, for example tenancy agreements, employment contracts and purchase contracts. The founding of companies is also in the OR.

The Criminal Code (StGB) sets out what a criminal offence is and what punishment it carries, for example a fine or prison. The Federal Act on Debt Enforcement and Bankruptcy (SchKG) governs how debts can be collected. The Federal Charter of 1291 is an old alliance of the first cantons, not a constitution.

key_terms.definition: Federal Constitution: the highest law of Switzerland, with the fundamental rights and the rules for the state.
Civil Code: governs persons, family, marriage, divorce, inheritance and property.
Code of Obligations: governs contracts such as tenancy, employment and purchase, and also companies.
Criminal Code: governs criminal offences and punishments such as fines or prison.

laws_codes.mnemonic: ZGB = living together and family. OR = contracts. StGB = punishments.

prohibitions.title: What is prohibited and what is protected
intro: The Federal Constitution protects the dignity and the life of every person. That is why torture and any cruel or inhuman treatment are prohibited. The death penalty is also prohibited. Other punishments are allowed, for example a fine, prison or community service. The police may not sentence anyone to prison. Anyone who does not agree with a punishment can let a court decide.

Freedom of opinion is broad. You may criticise the Federal Council, take part in demonstrations and wear religious symbols. But there are limits. It is prohibited to publicly make false claims about a person that damage their reputation. It is also prohibited to publicly demean people because of their origin or religion. That is discrimination and a criminal offence.

Privacy is protected. You may only publish private information about a person if they agree or if a law allows it. In Switzerland you may only be married to one person at a time. Anyone who has two marriages commits a criminal offence. Living together unmarried, on the other hand, is allowed.

Swiss citizens may not be expelled from Switzerland. They may only be extradited to another state if they themselves agree. There is an exception for trials before international criminal courts: Switzerland can also hand over its own citizens to them.

key_terms.definition: Prohibition of torture: nobody may be tortured or treated inhumanely.
Defamation: publicly claiming something that damages a person's reputation; this is a criminal offence.
Data protection: protection of a person's private information against misuse.
Extradition: a state hands a person over to another state for criminal proceedings.

duties.title: Taxes, registration, health insurance
intro: Anyone who lives in Switzerland has not only rights but also obligations. They apply to all residents, with or without a Swiss passport. Three important obligations are: paying taxes, registering with the municipality and having health insurance. In addition, everyone must obey the laws.

Anyone who moves or comes to Switzerland for the first time must register with the municipality. You do this at the residents' registration office, usually within 14 days. Anyone who moves away deregisters. Anyone who has income or assets must pay taxes. The taxes go to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality. For many foreigners, the tax is deducted directly from their wages.

All people who live in Switzerland must be insured with a health insurance fund. Anyone who moves here must take out the insurance within three months. The following, however, are not obligations: a bank account, a telephone, a driving licence, a Half Fare travelcard (Halbtax), theft insurance or membership of a church. But children must attend compulsory school.

key_terms.definition: Residents' registration office: the municipal office where you register and deregister.
Basic insurance: the compulsory health insurance for everyone who lives in Switzerland.
Withholding tax on wages: tax that the employer deducts directly from wages, mainly for foreigners without a C permit.

military_service.title: Military service, civilian service and civil protection service
intro: In Switzerland, military service is compulsory. Every Swiss man must do service, usually from about the age of 19 and up to a certain age. For Swiss women, military service is voluntary. Foreigners without Swiss citizenship do not have to do any service. The army protects the country and also helps in disasters.

Anyone who is fit for military service but cannot reconcile armed service with their conscience may do civilian service. So civilian service is a substitute for military service. It lasts one and a half times as long. People doing civilian service work, for example, in hospitals, care homes, schools or in environmental protection.

Anyone who is not fit for military service but is fit for civil protection does civil protection service. Civil protection helps in disasters and emergencies. Anyone who does no service at all pays a substitute charge every year, the military service exemption tax. It is three percent of taxable income, but at least 400 francs. Anyone who is doing service receives money from the income compensation scheme for that time.

key_terms.definition: Military service: service in the army, compulsory for Swiss men.
Civilian service: substitute for military service for men who cannot serve in the army for reasons of conscience.
Civil protection: service to protect the population in disasters, for men who are not fit for military service.
Military service exemption tax: money that Swiss men pay if they do not do any service.

three_pillars.title: The three pillars
intro: The pension system in Switzerland rests on three pillars. Each pillar has its own task. Together they are meant to ensure that you have enough money to live on in old age, in case of invalidity or after the death of a partner. This is also called the three-pillar system.

The first pillar is state pension provision: the AHV (old-age and survivors' insurance) together with the IV (invalidity insurance). It is compulsory for everyone and is meant to cover basic needs. The second pillar is occupational pension provision, in other words the pension fund. Employees and employers pay in together. It is meant to help people keep their usual standard of living.

The third pillar is private pension provision. Here you save voluntarily yourself, for example in a pillar 3a account. You get tax deductions for this. That way you have extra money in old age. In principle, you can only withdraw the money in a pillar 3a account from the age of 60. People who only have the AHV and a pension fund often have to live on less money in old age than before.

key_terms.definition: First pillar: state pension provision with the AHV and IV, compulsory for everyone.
Second pillar: occupational pension provision, also called the pension fund or BVG.
Third pillar: voluntary private pension provision, for example pillar 3a.

three_pillars.mnemonic: State, job, self: 1st pillar from the state (AHV), 2nd pillar through your job (pension fund), 3rd pillar you save yourself.

ahv_iv.title: AHV, IV and supplementary benefits
intro: The AHV is the most important social insurance in Switzerland. AHV stands for old-age and survivors' insurance. It pays a pension in old age. It also pays the survivors: these are widows, widowers and orphans when someone dies. The AHV is compulsory for everyone who lives or works in Switzerland.

Closely linked to the AHV is the IV, the invalidity insurance. It helps people who can no longer work, or can only work part of the time, because of illness or an accident. First, the IV tries to bring the person back into working life. Only if that is not possible does it pay a pension. Contributions to the AHV and IV are deducted directly from wages.

The standard retirement age is now called the reference age. It is 65. For women, it has been rising step by step from 64 to 65 since the AHV 21 reform. From 2028, 65 applies to everyone. In addition, from December 2026 there is a 13th AHV pension payment each year.

Sometimes the AHV or IV pension is not enough for the bare necessities. Then there are supplementary benefits (EL). They help if, despite a pension, you do not reach the subsistence minimum. Supplementary benefits are not a gift but a right. However, you must apply for them. They are not paid for by wage contributions but with tax money from the Confederation and the cantons.

key_terms.definition: Old-age and survivors' insurance: it pays pensions in old age and to survivors.
Invalidity insurance: it helps people who can no longer work fully because of illness or an accident.
Reference age: the standard retirement age, now 65.
Supplementary benefits: extra money if the pension is not enough for the subsistence minimum.

ahv_iv.mnemonic: AHV: old age and survivors. IV: invalidity. EL: a supplement when it is not enough.

social_insurance.title: Unemployment and accident insurance
intro: Social insurance protects against the financial consequences of major risks in life. These include old age, invalidity, illness, accident and unemployment. Many social insurances are compulsory. The contributions are often deducted directly from wages. Theft, floods or burglary are not a matter for social insurance. There are private insurances for these.

Anyone who loses their job gets money from unemployment insurance (ALV). All employees pay unemployment insurance contributions from their wages, including apprentices and older people. Anyone who has reached retirement age no longer pays these contributions. Anyone who becomes unemployed registers with the RAV. RAV stands for regional employment centre. It helps with looking for a job and checks your efforts.

All employees are insured against accidents. The occupational accident insurance pays for accidents at work, for example the hospital costs. The employer pays this premium. Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week is also insured in their free time (non-occupational accident). Employees pay this part through a deduction from their wages.

key_terms.definition: Unemployment insurance: it pays daily allowances if you lose your job.
Regional employment centre: this is where you register if you become unemployed.
Occupational accident insurance: it pays for accidents at work; the employer pays the premium.

social_insurance.mnemonic: RAV: this is where work is arranged (Arbeitsvermittlung).

health_insurance.title: Health insurance fund and BAG
intro: In Switzerland, every person who lives here must have health insurance. This applies to children, adults and older people, whatever their nationality. After moving here, you have three months to get insured. A baby must also be insured at the latest three months after birth. The baby is then insured retroactively from birth.

The obligation applies to basic insurance, the compulsory health care insurance. Its benefits are set by law and are the same at all health insurance funds. You can freely choose your health insurance fund and change it every year. Only people who do not get insured are assigned to a fund by a cantonal office. Supplementary insurance, for example for the dentist or alternative medicine, is voluntary.

At federal level, the BAG, the Federal Office of Public Health, is responsible for health. It supervises health insurance and approves the premiums. It also provides information on health topics, for example during epidemics. The health insurance funds themselves are not public offices. They are private insurers that must follow the rules of the Confederation.

key_terms.definition: Compulsory health care insurance: the basic insurance that all residents must have.
Supplementary insurance: voluntary insurance for services that basic insurance does not pay for.
Federal Office of Public Health: the health authority of the Confederation.

health_insurance.mnemonic: Three months: that is how long you have to insure yourself or your baby.

employment.title: Employment contract, notice, maternity
intro: Anyone who starts a job concludes an employment contract with the employer. It sets out, for example, the wage, the working hours, the holidays and the notice period. Anyone who wants to end an employment relationship must give notice and respect the notice period. It is best to give notice in writing by registered letter or to have receipt confirmed. That way you can prove the notice.

At the end of the job, or during it, you can ask for a reference letter. In it, the employer writes how you worked and behaved. The reference letter is important for later job applications. For a public office, for example on the municipal council or as a judge, the employer must give time off. The wage continues to be paid for this for a certain time.

Pregnant women are specially protected. After the probationary period, they may not be dismissed during pregnancy and for 16 weeks after the birth. After the birth, working mothers have 14 weeks of maternity leave. They receive 80 percent of their wage, up to a maximum of 220 francs per day. Condition: they were previously insured for at least 9 months and in paid work for 5 months.

key_terms.definition: Employment contract: contract between employer and employee on wages, working hours and other conditions.
Notice period: the time between giving notice and the end of the employment relationship.
Reference letter from an employer: written assessment of performance and conduct by the employer.
Maternity leave: 14 weeks of paid leave for working mothers after the birth.

employment.mnemonic: 14 weeks of leave, 16 weeks of protection against dismissal after the birth.

labour_disputes.title: Disputes at work
intro: Sometimes there are disputes at work. For example, the employer pays too little, or dismisses someone without reason. First, you should talk to the employer and put your objections in writing. If that does not help, there are legal options. You do not simply have to accept such a dispute.

For questions about employment law, you can turn to a trade union if you are a member. Lawyers and legal advice centres also help. The labour court is responsible for disputes arising from the employment contract. Before that, there is usually an attempt at conciliation. Up to an amount in dispute of 30 000 francs, the proceedings cost no court fees.

The police are not responsible for disputes at work. Wages and dismissal are matters of civil law, in other words disputes between private parties. Private problems, for example with the neighbours or with taxes, do not belong before the labour court either. Also important: simply no longer going to work is risky. By doing so, you may breach the contract yourself. It is better to get advice first, for example from a trade union.

key_terms.definition: Labour court: court for disputes between employer and employee arising from the employment relationship.
Trade union: organisation that represents the interests of employees and advises its members.

vocational.title: Vocational education and career information
intro: Most young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after compulsory school. They learn at a company and also attend a vocational school. This is called dual vocational education and training. Anyone who wants to choose or change their occupation can get free advice. This applies to young people and to adults.

Information about apprenticeships, occupations and continuing education is available at the career information centre, BIZ for short. Young people and adults can look at documents and ask questions there without an appointment. In the canton of Zurich there are BIZ centres in several places, for example in Oerlikon, Winterthur and Kloten. A vocational training centre (Berufsbildungszentrum) is a place where various offerings in vocational education come together, for example a vocational school and continuing education courses.

key_terms.definition: Career information centre: here you get information and advice on occupations, apprenticeships and continuing education.
Vocational training centre: a location with various offerings in vocational education.
Apprenticeship: training at a company with lessons at a vocational school.

taxes.title: Taxes and the tax return
intro: With taxes, the state pays for its tasks, for example schools, roads, the police and social assistance. You pay taxes to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality. How much you pay depends on your taxable income and your assets. Anyone who earns or owns more pays more. Nationality or party membership play no role.

Once a year you fill in the tax return. In it, you show the tax authority your financial situation: income, assets, debts and deductions. After that you receive the tax bill. If you do not agree with it, you can lodge an objection in writing. The deadline is usually 30 days.

There are also other taxes. Value added tax (MWST) is included in the price of many goods and services. The standard rate is currently 8.1 percent. You pay it when shopping without noticing it directly. Anyone who has a dog pays a dog tax to the municipality every year. The dog must also be registered.

key_terms.definition: Tax return: form with which you declare your income and assets to the tax authority.
Objection: a written challenge to a decision of the authority, for example to the tax bill.
Value added tax: tax that is included in the price of goods and services.
Dog tax: annual charge paid to the municipality for each dog.

family_support.title: Child allowances and tax deductions
intro: The state supports families with children. The most important help is family allowances. Employees and self-employed people are entitled to them, for each child. Parents who are not in paid work can also receive them. The money comes via the employer or the family compensation fund. You receive it every month together with your wages.

There are two types: the child allowance is paid up to the age of 16. In the canton of Zurich it is 215 francs per month, and 268 francs from the age of 12. The education allowance is paid for young people in education or training, from 15 up to a maximum of 25. It is 268 francs per month (as of 2026).

Families also get relief through taxes. For each child, you may deduct an amount from your income. You can also deduct childcare costs. That way families pay less tax. People on a low income can also get a reduction in their health insurance premiums. However, there are no free train journeys or cheaper food for families.

key_terms.definition: Family allowances: monthly payments for children, as a child allowance or an education allowance.
Child allowance: monthly allowance for children up to the age of 16.
Tax deduction: an amount you may deduct from your taxable income, for example for children.

marriage.title: Marriage, divorce, family name
intro: Two people may marry if they are at least 18 years old and capable of judgement. Capable of judgement means: you understand what you are doing. They may not already be married. They may also not be closely related, so not parent and child or brother and sister. Since 2022, two women or two men may also marry. Income, place of residence or the parents' consent play no role.

Before the wedding, the couple together register their intention to marry at the civil registry office. The office checks the requirements. This is called the preparatory procedure. After that, the civil wedding takes place. A church wedding is voluntary and may only take place after the civil wedding. The wedding usually takes place in the wedding room of the civil registry office.

For names, the rule is: each person can keep their name. Or the couple chooses one of their birth names (the name before the first marriage) as their common family name. If they have no common name, the parents decide at the wedding which name the children will get. A divorce can be requested by the wife, the husband or both together.

key_terms.definition: Civil registry office: office that records births, marriages and deaths and performs weddings.
Capable of judgement: able to understand what you are doing and to act accordingly.
Birth name: the name you had before your first marriage.

family_law.title: Bringing up children and the time-limit model
intro: Bringing up children is mainly the task of the parents. They provide care, education and protection. School and the state support the parents but do not replace them. Only if a child's well-being is at risk does an authority step in: the child and adult protection authority (KESB).

Since 2002, abortion has been regulated by the time-limit model (Fristenlösung). The people accepted it on 2 June 2002. In the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, the woman decides herself whether she wants to keep the child. She must request the abortion in writing and state that she is in a situation of distress. A doctor advises her beforehand. The husband's consent is not needed.

key_terms.definition: Time-limit model: rule under which an abortion in the first 12 weeks is not punishable.
Child and adult protection authority: it protects children when their well-being is at risk.

family_law.mnemonic: Fristenlösung: the time limit (Frist) is 12 weeks.

housing.title: Renting
intro: Most people in Switzerland live in rented housing. The tenancy agreement sets out the rights and obligations of the tenant and the landlord. It contains, for example, the rent, the service charges, the notice periods and the house rules. The contract does not decide how you furnish the flat or what you cook.

The flat is private. But the landlord may enter it if he has a good reason. Examples are repairs, a viewing for new tenants or a sale. He must announce the visit in good time. The tenant must then let him in. Other people, such as the employer or the postal worker, do not have this right.

The Tenants' Association (Mieterinnen- und Mieterverband) helps with problems with the landlord. It is an interest group: it advises its members and works politically for tenants. In a dispute, you can turn to the conciliation authority for tenancy matters. It is free of charge and is not part of the association.

key_terms.definition: Tenancy agreement: contract for renting a flat, with the rights and obligations of both sides.
Tenants' Association: association that represents the interests of tenants.
Conciliation authority: state office that mediates in disputes between tenant and landlord.

school.title: Compulsory school
intro: In Switzerland, all children must go to school. In most cantons, compulsory schooling lasts 11 years. It begins at about the age of 4 with two years of kindergarten. Then come 6 years of primary school and 3 years of lower secondary school. This is set out in the HarmoS Agreement, an agreement between the cantons. The canton of Zurich applies it too.

State schools (Volksschule) are a matter for the cantons and municipalities. They are free of charge. The school management or the school board decides which class a child is placed in. The parents cannot simply choose a class. The children or the paediatrician do not decide this either. The school takes into account, for example, the size of the classes and the way to school.

Things that are not compulsory include day-care centres, baccalaureate school (Gymnasium, Maturitätsschule) and continuing education. After compulsory school, most young people do an apprenticeship. Others attend a baccalaureate school and then perhaps a university. With a vocational baccalaureate, you can also study after an apprenticeship.

key_terms.definition: Compulsory school: the 11 years of compulsory schooling in kindergarten, primary school and lower secondary school.
School board: municipal authority that supervises the state school.
Agreement between the cantons that harmonises the length and goals of schooling.

school.mnemonic: 2 + 6 + 3 = 11: kindergarten, primary school, lower secondary school.

associations.title: Associations
intro: In Switzerland there are very many associations and clubs, for example for sport, music or culture. Many people volunteer in them. The Constitution guarantees freedom of association. This means: every person may found an association, join an association or leave it. There are no conditions such as income, sex or a minimum age of 21.

Two people are enough to found an association. They write articles of association, in other words the rules of the association. These contain the purpose, the finances and the bodies such as the committee and the general meeting. Associations are important for living together and for integration. One example is the neighbourhood association (Quartierverein): it represents the interests of the people in a neighbourhood.

key_terms.definition: Freedom of association: fundamental right to found associations, join them or stay out of them.
Articles of association: the written rules of an association with its purpose and organisation.

emergency.title: Emergency numbers and sirens
intro: In an emergency, you must quickly dial the right number. 117 is the police emergency number. 118 is the fire service. 144 is the ambulance service, in other words emergency medical services with an ambulance. The European emergency number 112 also works. Rega, the helicopter rescue service, can be reached on 1414. Emergency numbers are free of charge.

When there is great danger to the population, for example in a chemical accident, the sirens sound. This is the general alarm. You should then listen to the radio or open the Alertswiss app and follow the instructions of the authorities. You should also inform your neighbours. Once a year, in February, the sirens are tested.

key_terms.definition: 117: emergency number of the police.
144: emergency number of the ambulance service.
General alarm: siren alarm in case of danger; listen to the radio, follow instructions, inform your neighbours.

emergency.mnemonic: Remember the order: 117 police, 118 fire service, 144 ambulance. When the sirens sound: turn on the radio.

driving.title: Driving licence
intro: To drive a car or a motorcycle, you need a driving licence (Führerausweis, often called Fahrausweis). Anyone who seriously breaks the traffic rules can lose it. The Road Traffic Office can then withdraw the licence for a certain time. During this time you may no longer drive. In serious cases you then have to attend courses or take a test.

An important reason for withdrawal is driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. From 0.5 per mille you may no longer drive. From 0.8 per mille, the licence is withdrawn for at least three months. For new drivers and professional drivers, practically zero per mille (0.1) applies. For drugs, there is zero tolerance. Parking incorrectly or using the horn, on the other hand, only costs a fine.

key_terms.definition: Withdrawal of the driving licence: the authority takes the driving licence away for a certain time.
Per mille: measure of the alcohol in the blood. From 0.5 per mille, driving is prohibited.

early_history.title: Helvetii and Romans
intro: More than 2000 years ago, Celtic peoples lived in the area of present-day Switzerland. The most important people were the Helvetii. They lived mainly in the Plateau between the Jura, the Alps and the Rhine. Switzerland is still named after them today: in Latin it is called «Helvetia». The CH on car number plates also comes from this. It stands for «Confoederatio Helvetica», in other words the Helvetic Confederation.

In 58 BC, the Helvetii wanted to emigrate westwards into present-day France. The Roman general Julius Caesar defeated them at Bibracte and sent them back. After that, the area of Switzerland came under Roman rule. The Romans stayed for around 400 years. They built roads, towns, temples and theatres.

The capital of the Helvetii in Roman times was Aventicum, present-day Avenches in the canton of Vaud. A large amphitheatre still stands there today. This is a round arena with rows of seats. There people watched animal hunts and gladiator fights. Other Roman sites are Augusta Raurica (Augst near Basel) and the legionary camp of Vindonissa (Windisch).

key_terms.definition: Helvetii: a Celtic people who lived in the Plateau of present-day Switzerland in Roman times.
Aventicum: Roman capital of the Helvetii, today Avenches (VD), with a well-preserved amphitheatre.
Amphitheatre: a round or oval Roman arena with rows of seats for games and fights.

early_history.mnemonic: CH on the car = «Confoederatio Helvetica»: the Helvetii are in the name of Switzerland.

founding_1291.title: 1291, the Rütli and William Tell
intro: At the beginning of August 1291, three valley communities on Lake Lucerne formed an alliance: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. They are called the founding cantons (Urkantone). Today Unterwalden is divided into two cantons: Obwalden and Nidwalden. The alliance is recorded in a document in Latin, the Federal Charter. In it, the valley communities promised each other mutual help and wanted to settle disputes peacefully.

For a long time, the Federal Charter lay forgotten in an archive. Only in 1891, for the 600th anniversary, was 1291 made the official founding year of the Confederation. Before that, 1307 was often seen as the founding year. In 1891, people celebrated on 1 August for the first time. Since 1899, Switzerland has celebrated its National Day every year on 1 August. Historians today say: the alliance of 1291 was one of many alliances to keep the peace, not the real founding of a state. For the test: 1291, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden.

According to legend, men from the three founding cantons swore an oath of alliance against foreign bailiffs on the Rütli. The Rütli is a meadow above Lake Uri. This Rütli oath is not proven by documents. Even so, the Rütli is today an important place of remembrance for the alliance of the founding cantons. Every year there is a 1 August celebration there.

William Tell is also a legendary figure. The story goes: the bailiff Gessler forced Tell to shoot an apple off his son's head with a crossbow. Later, Tell killed the bailiff. The legend first appears in the «White Book of Sarnen» (around 1470). It became famous through the play «William Tell» by Friedrich Schiller (1804). Tell stands for the fight against foreign rulers.

key_terms.definition: Founding cantons: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, which formed an alliance in 1291.
Federal Charter: the document of 1291 in which the founding cantons recorded their alliance.
Rütli: meadow on Lake Uri that commemorates the alliance of the founding cantons (place of the legendary Rütli oath).
Legend: an old story that is passed on but is not historically proven.

founding_1291.mnemonic: «U-S-U»: Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden. 1291 in the Federal Charter, celebrated on 1 August.

marignano.title: Marignano 1515
intro: In the 15th century, the Confederates were militarily very strong. They conquered new territories and fought as mercenaries for foreign rulers. At the beginning of the 16th century, they fought for control of Milan in northern Italy. In doing so, they came into conflict with the King of France.

On 13 and 14 September 1515, the Confederates lost the Battle of Marignano, near Milan, against the French king Francis I. Thousands of Confederates died. In 1516, the Confederates concluded the «Perpetual Peace» with France. They gave up Milan. After that, the Confederation abandoned its policy of conquest. The time of great joint conquests was over.

Later, Marignano was often seen as the beginning of Swiss neutrality. Historians today are more careful: Swiss mercenaries fought in foreign armies for a long time afterwards. Neutrality was only recognised in 1815. Important for the test: the most important consequence of Marignano was the end of the policy of conquest.

key_terms.definition: Marignano: place near Milan where the Confederates lost against France in 1515.
Mercenaries: soldiers who fight for a foreign ruler in return for payment.
Conquest: taking over a foreign territory by force.

reformation.title: The Reformation
intro: In the 16th century, many people in Europe wanted to renew the Catholic Church. For example, they criticised the fact that people could buy their way out of their sins with money. This religious movement is called the Reformation. It began in 1517 in Germany with Martin Luther. It gave rise to the Protestant faith, in Switzerland usually called «Reformed» or «Evangelical Reformed».

In Switzerland, Huldrych (Ulrich) Zwingli was the most important reformer. From 1519 he preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich. From 1523, Zurich introduced the Reformation. Later, Bern and Basel, for example, followed. In Geneva, John Calvin was active from 1536. His teaching spread to many countries.

Not all cantons became Reformed. Central Switzerland, for example, remained Catholic. So the Reformation split the Confederation into two denominations. This led to wars, the Kappel Wars. In 1531, Zwingli died in the Battle of Kappel. The tensions between Catholics and Reformed shaped Switzerland until well into the 19th century.

key_terms.definition: Reformation: religious renewal movement in the 16th century that gave rise to the Protestant churches.
Protestant / Reformed: the faith that arose with the Reformation; in Switzerland the church is usually called Evangelical Reformed.
Denomination: a branch of faith within Christianity, for example Catholic or Reformed.

reformation.mnemonic: Zwingli in Zurich, Calvin in Geneva: both cities are centres of the Reformation.

helvetic_republic.title: 1798: the French and Napoleon
intro: After the French Revolution of 1789, France wanted to spread its ideas and its power. At the beginning of 1798, French troops marched into the Confederation. On 5 March 1798, Bern fell. The Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed. France mainly wanted to control the Alpine passes to Italy, and wanted money for its wars and Swiss soldiers.

In April 1798, the Helvetic Republic was created. It was a centralised state: the government sat in one place and decided everything. The cantons were now only administrative districts. New were equal rights for all citizens. The subject territories became free. But many people rejected the centralised state. There were uprisings.

The best-known ruler of this time was Napoleon Bonaparte. In 1798 he was still a general. From 1799 he ruled France. In 1803, with the Act of Mediation, he gave Switzerland a new order. The cantons became more independent again. New cantons such as Aargau, Thurgau, St. Gallen, Ticino and Vaud were created. In the test, the answer is usually: Napoleon and the French invasion.

key_terms.definition: Helvetic Republic: the centralised state that France set up in Switzerland from 1798 to 1803.
Centralised state: a state in which a central government decides everything and the regions have little power.
Act of Mediation: constitution that Napoleon gave Switzerland in 1803; it made the cantons stronger again.

helvetic_republic.mnemonic: 1798: the French come, the centralised state comes. 1803: Napoleon gives the cantons more power again.

neutrality.title: Neutrality since 1815
intro: Being neutral means: Switzerland does not get involved in armed conflicts, in other words wars, between other states. It does not help any warring party with soldiers. It does not let foreign troops pass through its territory. Switzerland protects its neutrality with its own army. That is why people speak of armed neutrality.

Neutral does not mean that Switzerland stays alone. It concludes many treaties with other states, including states at war. It is a member of the UN and trades with the whole world. It also offers «good offices», for example as a venue for peace talks.

After the Napoleonic wars, the European great powers reorganised Europe. This happened at the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815. There they established that Switzerland should remain neutral. On 20 November 1815 in Paris, the great powers recognised Switzerland's «perpetual neutrality». At the same time, Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel joined as new cantons.

key_terms.definition: Neutrality: a state does not take part in wars between other states.
Congress of Vienna: conference of the European powers in 1814/1815 that reorganised Europe after Napoleon.
Armed neutrality: Switzerland is neutral but defends itself with its own army.

neutrality.mnemonic: 1815 in Vienna: the great powers say «neutral», and Switzerland has stayed that way ever since.

founding_1848.title: Sonderbund War and the federal state of 1848
intro: At the beginning of the 19th century, Switzerland was a loose alliance of cantons. There was a dispute between two groups. The Liberals, mainly in Reformed cantons, wanted a stronger common state. The Catholic-conservative cantons wanted to keep their independence. In 1845 they formed their own alliance: the Sonderbund (separate alliance). It included seven cantons, for example Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Fribourg.

In November 1847, the Sonderbund War broke out: Catholics against Liberals. The troops of the Diet (Tagsatzung) under General Guillaume-Henri Dufour won after about three weeks. Dufour wanted as few victims as possible. Fewer than a hundred people died. It was the last war on Swiss soil. Afterwards, the winners were able to build a new, common state.

On 12 September 1848, the new Federal Constitution came into force. Switzerland became a federalist federal state. Federalist means: the cantons keep a lot of their own power, but there is a common Confederation. New were the Federal Council and the Parliament with the National Council and the Council of States. The Confederation was now responsible for money. In 1850 the franc came as the common currency. That is why 1848 is seen as the founding of modern Switzerland.

key_terms.definition: Sonderbund (separate alliance): alliance of seven Catholic-conservative cantons from 1845.
Sonderbund War: short civil war in 1847 between Liberals and Catholic cantons.
Federal state: a state made up of member states (cantons) that decide a lot themselves, with a common government.
Federalist: power is shared between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.

founding_1848.mnemonic: 1847 war, 1848 constitution: the federal state grows out of the conflict.

industrialisation.title: From agrarian state to industrial state
intro: Around 1800, most people in Switzerland lived from agriculture. In the 19th century, Switzerland changed from an agrarian state into an industrial state. Industrialisation means: goods are made with machines in factories instead of by hand. The basis was an invention from England: the steam engine. In the 18th century, James Watt improved it so that it could drive machines in factories. This started industrialisation in Europe in the 19th century.

At first, the textile industry was the most important. In 1802, the first large mechanical cotton spinning mill opened near Winterthur. In Switzerland, factories often ran on water power. Later came the machine industry, chemicals and watches. Switzerland had no colonies of its own. But Swiss companies bought raw materials such as cotton from the colonies of other countries. This helped Switzerland to become an industrial nation.

Many children also worked in the factories, often 12 to 14 hours a day. That is why they could not go to school. In 1877, the people accepted the federal Factory Act. It banned factory work for children under 14 and limited the working day to 11 hours.

Even so, many people remained poor. In the 19th century, crop failures, hunger and unemployment drove many Swiss people abroad, mainly to North and South America. Switzerland was then a country of emigration. Today it is the other way round: many people immigrate to Switzerland because there is work here.

key_terms.definition: Industrialisation: the change from manual work to production with machines in factories.
Agrarian state: a country in which most people live from agriculture.
Textile industry: industry that produces yarn and fabrics, for example from cotton.
Factory Act of 1877: first national law to protect workers; it banned factory work for children under 14.

industrialisation.mnemonic: Thread before steel: in Switzerland, industry began with textiles.

general_strike.title: National general strike of 1918
intro: During the First World War (1914 to 1918), many workers in Switzerland were badly off. Prices rose sharply, wages hardly at all. There was not enough food. Many people worked ten hours a day, six days a week. Many families could hardly pay for rent and food. The soldiers at the border also received little pay. Discontent grew, and there were more and more strikes.

In November 1918, the trade unions and the Social Democratic Party called a national general strike (Landesstreik). This is a strike across the whole country. Around 250 000 people stopped work. Trains, factories and many businesses came to a standstill. The Federal Council sent the army into the cities. After three days, the strike leaders called off the strike to avoid violence.

The strikers had nine demands, for example the 48-hour week, an old-age insurance and women's suffrage. Some demands were soon met: the 48-hour week came in 1919. From 1919, the National Council was elected by proportional representation. Other demands only came much later: the AHV in 1948, women's suffrage in 1971.

key_terms.definition: National general strike: the general strike in November 1918 throughout Switzerland.
48-hour week: limit on working time to 48 hours per week, introduced in 1919.

ww2.title: Second World War
intro: During the Second World War (1939 to 1945), Switzerland remained neutral. It fought neither for the Allies (for example the USA, Great Britain, the Soviet Union) nor for the Axis powers (Germany, Italy, Japan). Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by Germany and Italy. The army under General Henri Guisan prepared to defend itself in the Alps. This is called the «Réduit».

But neutral did not mean: no contacts. Switzerland had political and economic relations with all sides. It depended on coal and food from abroad. Swiss companies supplied weapons and machines, above all to Germany. The National Bank bought German gold. Transit between Germany and Italy went through Switzerland.

Switzerland took in around 60 000 civilian refugees. But it also turned many away, including many Jewish people. From 1942, the border was largely closed to them. A commission of experts (Bergier Commission) examined this period and clearly criticised the refugee policy in 1999.

key_terms.definition: Allies: the states that fought against Germany, for example the USA, Great Britain and the Soviet Union.
Axis powers: Germany, Italy and Japan with their allies.
Réduit: the Swiss army's plan to defend itself in the Alps.

migration_history.title: Immigration and the Schwarzenbach initiative
intro: After the Second World War, the economy grew strongly. Switzerland needed many workers. In 1948 it concluded an agreement with Italy. After that, mainly Italians came. They worked in construction, in factories and in hotels. Many only had a permit as a seasonal worker (Saisonnier): they were allowed to stay for a few months and could not bring their family. Later, people also came from Spain, Portugal, Yugoslavia and Turkey.

Not everyone agreed with immigration. People spoke of «Überfremdung» (foreign infiltration). In 1970 Switzerland voted on the Schwarzenbach initiative, named after the politician James Schwarzenbach. It wanted to limit the number of foreigners to a maximum of 10 percent in every canton except Geneva. Hundreds of thousands would have had to leave the country. The initiative was narrowly rejected with 54 percent voting no.

In the 1990s Yugoslavia broke apart. There were wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and later in Kosovo. Many people fled from these wars to Switzerland. Some already had relatives here who had come earlier as workers. Switzerland took in, for example, many thousands of people displaced by the war in Bosnia. Today many of their families are firmly settled in Switzerland.

key_terms.definition: Seasonal worker: a foreign worker who was only allowed to work in Switzerland for one season (a few months).
Schwarzenbach initiative: popular initiative of 1970 that wanted to limit the number of foreigners; it was rejected.
Foreign infiltration: a political slogan for the fear that there are too many foreigners.

prosperity.title: Prosperity and AHV
intro: After the Second World War, Switzerland was not destroyed. The factories could produce immediately. In the 1950s and especially in the 1960s, the economy grew very strongly. This period is called the economic boom (Hochkonjunktur). There was more work than there were workers. Wages rose significantly, especially quickly in the 1960s. The standard of living rose sharply for many people.

Many families could now afford things that had been luxuries before: a car, a fridge, a washing machine, a television or holidays. Switzerland became a consumer society. That means: people buy much more than just the bare necessities. Working-class families also had more money now. Before, for example in the crisis of the 1930s, many people were unemployed and poor.

Social security also improved. In 1947 the people approved the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV). It has paid pensions since 1 January 1948. The AHV is a state insurance for everyone. It pays money to old people and to survivors, that is widows, widowers and orphans. To this day it is the most important social insurance in Switzerland.

key_terms.definition: Standard of living: how well people can live, for example how much they can afford.
Economic boom: a long period of strong economic growth, in Switzerland roughly 1950 to 1973.
AHV: old-age and survivors' insurance, the state pension since 1948.

prosperity.mnemonic: AHV 1948: after the war there is a pension for everyone.

jura.title: The youngest canton: Jura
intro: Jura is the youngest canton in Switzerland. The area used to belong to the Prince-Bishopric of Basel. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave it to the canton of Bern. The north of the Jura is French-speaking and Catholic. Bern is mostly German-speaking and Reformed. That is why many people from the Jura did not feel at home in Bern.

In the 20th century the conflict became stronger. People spoke of the Jura question. In 1974 the people in the northern Jura voted for a canton of their own. In 1978 the Swiss people and all cantons said yes. Since 1 January 1979, Jura has been an independent canton, the 26th in Switzerland. Its capital is Delémont (Delsberg). Since 2026 the town of Moutier has also belonged to the canton of Jura.

key_terms.definition: Canton of Jura: the youngest canton in Switzerland, independent since 1979, previously part of the canton of Bern.
Jura question: the long dispute over whether the Jura should belong to Bern or be a canton of its own.

women_rights.title: Women's suffrage and equal rights
intro: In Switzerland, women were not allowed to vote and elect for a long time. Because only men were allowed to vote, the men had to decide on it. In 1959 they still said no. On 7 February 1971 they said yes, with 66 percent. Since then, Swiss women have had the right to vote and elect at federal level. Many other countries in Europe had it decades earlier.

In some cantons it took even longer. The last canton was Appenzell Innerrhoden. There, in 1990, the Federal Supreme Court had to enforce women's suffrage. On 14 June 1981, the people added a new article to the Federal Constitution: men and women have equal rights. The article also demands equal pay for work of equal value.

In 1984 Parliament elected the first woman to the Federal Council: Elisabeth Kopp (FDP) from the canton of Zurich. She resigned in 1989. Later more women Federal Councillors followed, for example Ruth Dreifuss (1993), Ruth Metzler (1999) and Micheline Calmy-Rey (2002). In 1999 Ruth Dreifuss was the first woman President of the Confederation. Today women in the Federal Council and in Parliament are a matter of course.

key_terms.definition: Women's suffrage: the right of women to vote and elect; at federal level since 1971.
Equality article: article of the Constitution from 1981: men and women have equal rights.
Woman Federal Councillor: a woman in the national government; the first was Elisabeth Kopp (1984).

women_rights.mnemonic: 71, 81, 84: right to vote, equal rights, first woman Federal Councillor.

traditions.title: Jass, yodelling, Fasnacht, Chilbi
intro: Many Swiss traditions come from life in the countryside. Yodelling is one of them. When you yodel, you sing without words. The voice jumps quickly back and forth between a low chest voice and a high head voice. You do not need an instrument for it, only your own voice. Since 2025 Swiss yodelling has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

The most popular card game in Switzerland is called Jass. It has been played for centuries, often by four people in the family, in a club or in a restaurant. There are German and French Jass cards. Jass is considered Switzerland's national game. It is played with 36 cards. There are many variants; the best known is called «Schieber».

Fasnacht (carnival) is a festival before Lent in spring. Masks, costumes, loud music and parades through the streets are typical. The best known is the Basel Fasnacht. It starts on the Monday after Ash Wednesday at 4 a.m. with the «Morgestraich»: the street lights go out, and pipers and drummers march with colourful lanterns through the dark old town.

A «Chilbi» is a traditional fair, often for the anniversary of a church's consecration (Kirchweih). The word comes from «Kirchweih». There are merry-go-rounds, roller coasters, shooting galleries and stalls with sweets. Almost every village and town has a Chilbi once a year. Families, friends and neighbours meet there.

key_terms.definition: Yodelling: singing without words, where the voice switches quickly between low and high registers.
Jass: the traditional card game of Switzerland.
Carnival: a festival before Lent with masks, costumes, music and parades.
Morgestraich: the start of the Basel Fasnacht at 4 a.m. in the dark, with pipes and drums.
Chilbi: a traditional fair with merry-go-rounds and roller coasters, originally for the Kirchweih (church consecration festival).

traditions.mnemonic: Chilbi comes from «Kirchweih»: a festival for the whole village, today with roller coaster and merry-go-round.

sports.title: Schwingen, skiing, football, Federer
intro: Schwingen is a traditional Swiss sport. It is a form of wrestling. Two men or two women hold on to short trousers made of cloth and fight in a circle of sawdust. Whoever puts the other on their back wins. Every three years there is the big Federal Schwingen and Alpine Festival (Eidgenössisches Schwing- und Älplerfest). The winner is called «Schwingerkönig» (king of Schwingen).

In winter many people in Switzerland go skiing. The Alps offer many ski resorts, and many children learn to ski at school, for example at ski camp. But most people ski privately, not in a club. Successful ski racers are big stars in Switzerland.

The sport most people in Switzerland play in a sports club is football. The football association has hundreds of thousands of members. Almost every municipality has its own football club. The best-known Swiss athlete is the tennis player Roger Federer. He won 20 Grand Slam tournaments, for example Wimbledon eight times.

The circus is also part of entertainment. The largest circus in Switzerland is Circus Knie. It is also called the «Swiss National Circus» and tours many Swiss towns every year. The Knie family has run it for generations. In the ring, acrobats, clowns and animals show their skills.

key_terms.definition: Schwingen: traditional Swiss wrestling in sawdust.
King of Schwingen: the winner of the Federal Schwingen and Alpine Festival.
Club or association: a group of people who share a hobby, for example a sport.
Circus Knie: the largest circus in Switzerland, also called the «Swiss National Circus».

arts.title: Writers, artists, National Museum
intro: Switzerland has well-known writers. Johanna Spyri wrote the book «Heidi» in 1880. It tells the story of a girl who lives with her grandfather in the mountains of Graubünden. Heidi has been translated into more than 50 languages and often made into films. She is the most famous character in Swiss literature.

Max Frisch (1911-1991) and Friedrich Dürrenmatt (1921-1990) were important writers of the 20th century. Frisch wrote, for example, the novel «Homo faber». Dürrenmatt wrote the play «Der Besuch der alten Dame» (The Visit). Both criticised the society of their time and are still read in schools today.

Women artists from Switzerland are also internationally known. Sophie Taeuber-Arp was a pioneer of modern art. She was on the former 50-franc note. Pipilotti Rist makes video art today. Niki de Saint Phalle made large, colourful female figures, the «Nanas». One hangs in the hall of Zurich main station. She came from France and became Swiss by marrying the Swiss artist Jean Tinguely.

The Swiss National Museum (Landesmuseum) in Zurich stands next to the main station. It is the most important museum for Swiss history. It shows how Switzerland came into being: from the Middle Ages to today. The building looks like a castle. Art such as paintings by the Impressionists, on the other hand, can be seen at the Kunsthaus.

key_terms.definition: Johanna Spyri: Swiss writer who created the character «Heidi».
Max Frisch and Friedrich Dürrenmatt: the two best-known Swiss writers of the 20th century.
Swiss National Museum: museum in Zurich that shows the history of Switzerland.

arts.mnemonic: Frisch and Dürrenmatt: two men with a pen, not a brush. Taeuber-Arp, Rist, Saint Phalle: three women with brush and camera.

watch_industry.title: Watch industry
intro: For centuries Switzerland has been a world leader in the watch industry. Swiss watches are considered particularly precise and of high quality. Brands such as Rolex, Omega or Swatch are known all over the world. Watches are among Switzerland's most important export goods, after pharmaceuticals and machines.

Watchmaking began in Geneva in the 16th century. From there it spread to the Jura. The Jura Arc is the chain of hills in the north-west of Switzerland, for example in the cantons of Neuchâtel, Jura, Bern and Solothurn. During the long winter, the farmers there worked at home as watchmakers. To this day the Jura region is the centre of the Swiss watch industry.

Around 700 companies make watches in Switzerland. Many of them are small businesses with highly specialised experts. The «Swiss made» label is a sign of quality. Anyone who buys a watch with this label expects precision and a long life. Other sectors such as textiles or mining, on the other hand, are small in Switzerland.

key_terms.definition: Watch industry: the economic sector that makes and sells watches.
Jura Arc: hilly region in the north-west of Switzerland, the centre of watchmaking.
Swiss made: label for products that were largely made in Switzerland.

watch_industry.mnemonic: Jura and watches: in the long Jura winter, the farmers built watches.

economy.title: Pioneers, hydropower, pharmaceuticals
intro: In the 19th century Switzerland became a modern industrial country. An important person in this was the Zurich politician and entrepreneur Alfred Escher (1819-1882). He campaigned for building railways, for example the Gotthard railway. He helped found the ETH in Zurich in 1854/55. In 1856 he founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, which later became Credit Suisse.

Switzerland has hardly any mineral resources such as oil, coal or gold. Its most important natural resource is water. The Alps have many lakes, rivers and glaciers. They are used to run hydroelectric power stations. Hydropower supplies about 60 percent of Switzerland's electricity. Oil, gas and coal, on the other hand, Switzerland has to import.

Today the pharmaceutical and chemical industry is the most important export sector. Its centre is the Basel region. Large companies such as Roche and Novartis have their headquarters there. They are among the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. The industry grew out of dye factories on the Rhine. That is why Basel is known above all as a location for pharmaceuticals, not as a wine region.

key_terms.definition: Alfred Escher: Zurich pioneer of the 19th century: railways, ETH and Kreditanstalt.
ETH: Federal Institute of Technology, a well-known university in Zurich.
Hydropower: electricity generated with the power of flowing water.
Pharmaceutical industry: companies that develop and make medicines.

economy.mnemonic: Escher built the foundation: railway, bank, education (ETH).

transport.title: Railways and the Gotthard
intro: Switzerland is a railway country. It is said of its railway network that it is the densest in the world. That means: there are very many railway lines on a small area. Almost every village can be reached by train or bus. People in Switzerland travel more kilometres by train per year than in almost any other country.

The largest railway company is SBB. That stands for «Schweizerische Bundesbahnen» (Swiss Federal Railways). It belongs to the Confederation. There are also many smaller railway companies, for example BLS (Bern-Lötschberg-Simplon), SOB (Schweizerische Südostbahn) and SZU (Sihltal-Zürich-Uetliberg-Bahn). They all work together, and you can travel through the whole country with one ticket.

At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world. It runs from Erstfeld (canton of Uri) to Bodio (canton of Ticino) and was opened in 2016. The tunnel lies deep down in the mountain and is almost flat. This way freight and passenger trains get through the Alps faster and more easily.

key_terms.definition: SBB: Swiss Federal Railways, the largest railway company in Switzerland.
Gotthard Base Tunnel: 57 km long railway tunnel through the Alps, the longest in the world.
NEAT: New Rail Link through the Alps, the construction project with the large Alpine tunnels at the Gotthard and the Lötschberg.

transport.mnemonic: Gotthard: 57 km, opened in 2016. A world record.

international_orgs.title: Red Cross, UN, Geneva and international organisations
intro: Switzerland is host country to many international organisations. Most of them have their seat in Geneva. The European seat of the UN is there, and for example the World Health Organization WHO. The UN Human Rights Council also meets in Geneva. In 2006 it replaced the former UN Human Rights Commission, which was also in Geneva.

The oldest and best known is the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The Geneva businessman Henry Dunant founded it in 1863 with other people from Geneva. In 1859 in Italy he had seen the Battle of Solferino, where thousands of wounded soldiers died without help. The ICRC helps victims of war. Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. The ICRC still has its headquarters in Geneva today.

Switzerland has only been a member of the UN since 2002. The people approved joining in a popular vote. In the OSCE (Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe), Switzerland works for peace, above all in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. In 2026 Switzerland holds the chairmanship of the OSCE.

Sport and business also meet in Switzerland. The world football federation FIFA has its seat in Zurich. Many other sports federations are in Lausanne. Every year in January, the World Economic Forum (WEF) takes place in Davos. Politicians and company heads from all over the world meet there.

key_terms.definition: ICRC: International Committee of the Red Cross, founded in Geneva in 1863, helps victims of war.
UN: United Nations; Switzerland has been a member since 2002.
OSCE: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, works for peace.
WEF: World Economic Forum, an annual meeting of politics and business in Davos.
FIFA: world football federation with its seat in Zurich.

international_orgs.mnemonic: Geneva = Red Cross and UN, Zurich = FIFA, Davos = WEF.

eu_relations.title: Switzerland and the EU
intro: Switzerland is not a member of the European Union (EU). In 1992 the voters also rejected joining the European Economic Area (EEA). After that Switzerland looked for its own way: it concludes treaties with the EU on individual topics. These treaties are called «Bilateral Agreements» because two sides sign them.

The basis is the Bilateral Agreements I. The voters approved them in 2000. They regulate, for example, the free movement of persons, trade and transport. In 2004 the Bilaterals II followed, for example with Schengen. In 2026 Switzerland and the EU signed a new package, the «Bilaterals III». Parliament is currently debating it.

The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner. About half of exports go to the EU, and around 70 percent of imports come from the EU. The most important single EU country is Germany. The USA and China are also important partners, but all EU countries together are much more important.

The close connection can also be seen in everyday life. Many people live in France, Italy, Germany or Austria and work in Switzerland. They cross the border every day or every week. They are called cross-border commuters (Grenzgänger). There are especially many in Geneva, Basel and Ticino. Someone who only works in another canton, on the other hand, is a commuter (Pendler).

key_terms.definition: Bilateral Agreements: treaties between Switzerland and the EU on individual topics.
EEA: European Economic Area; Switzerland rejected joining in 1992.
Trading partner: a country or a group of countries with which you buy and sell goods.
Cross-border commuter: a person who lives abroad and works in Switzerland.

eu_relations.mnemonic: 1992 no to the EEA, 2000 yes to the Bilaterals: instead of joining, one treaty after another.

zh_government.title: Cantonal Government and directorates
intro: The government of the canton of Zurich is called the Cantonal Government (Regierungsrat). It is the executive, that is the executive power. The Cantonal Government has 7 members. They work full-time. Each member heads a directorate. A directorate is a large part of the cantonal administration, similar to a ministry.

The 7 directorates are: Directorate of Justice and Home Affairs, Directorate of Security, Directorate of Finance, Directorate of Economic Affairs, Directorate of Health, Directorate of Education and Directorate of Building. The Directorate of Building is responsible, for example, for cantonal roads, waters and the environment. There is no directorate for the military: the army is a matter for the Confederation.

The people elect the Cantonal Government directly, every 4 years. The majority voting system (Majorz) applies: the people with the most votes are elected. Neither the parties nor Parliament decide on the government. This is different from many other countries. The Federal Council, too, is not elected by the people, but by Parliament.

key_terms.definition: Cantonal Government: the government (executive) of the canton of Zurich with 7 members.
Directorate: an area of the cantonal administration headed by a member of the Cantonal Government, for example the Directorate of Building.
Executive: the executive power; it governs and runs the administration.
Majority voting system: whoever receives the most votes is elected.

zh_government.mnemonic: 7 members of the Cantonal Government, 7 directorates: each member has exactly one directorate.

zh_parliament.title: Cantonal Council and Council of States
intro: The parliament of the canton of Zurich is called the Cantonal Council (Kantonsrat). It is the legislature, that is the legislative power. The Cantonal Council has 180 members. It makes the cantonal laws and every year decides on the canton's budget. It also supervises the government and the administration. Some judges are also elected by the Cantonal Council.

The members of the Cantonal Council are elected by the people, every 4 years. The election is a proportional election (Proporz): each party receives as many seats as corresponds to its share of the votes. So the government does not appoint the members of parliament. In other cantons the parliament is often called the «Grand Council» (Grosser Rat). «Landtag» is the term used in Germany and Liechtenstein.

The Council of States is something different: it is a chamber of the Federal Parliament in Bern. Each full canton has 2 seats there, no matter how big it is. Zurich, too, has only 2 members of the Council of States, although it is the canton with the most inhabitants. In the National Council, on the other hand, Zurich has many seats, because they are distributed according to population.

key_terms.definition: Cantonal Council: the parliament of the canton of Zurich with 180 members.
Legislature: the legislative power, that is the parliament.
Proportional representation: the seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the votes.
Council of States: chamber of the Federal Parliament in which each full canton has 2 seats.

zh_parliament.mnemonic: Kantons-RAT = many people who deliberate (beraten) (180). Regierungs-RAT = few who govern (regieren) (7).

zh_canton_tasks.title: Tasks of the canton, districts, petition
intro: Switzerland has three levels: Confederation, cantons and municipalities. The cantons have their own laws, their own government and their own administration. The Confederation, on the other hand, is responsible for the army, foreign policy, customs and monetary policy. Treaties with the European Union are also concluded by the Confederation.

Typical tasks of the canton of Zurich are: university and universities of applied sciences, hospitals, police, courts and cantonal roads. The University of Zurich is a cantonal university. Together with the municipalities, the canton is also responsible for state schools (Volksschule). The cantonal administration implements the laws. It consists of 7 directorates with many offices, for example the Migration Office or the Road Traffic Office.

The canton of Zurich is divided into 12 districts, for example Zurich, Winterthur, Uster, Horgen or Meilen. Each municipality belongs to a district. A district is an administrative unit between the canton and the municipalities and has its own authorities. Each district has, for example, a district court. This way the cantonal administration is not only in the city of Zurich, but everywhere in the canton.

In the canton of Zurich, only Swiss citizens may vote and elect. But anyone may submit a petition, including foreigners and children. A petition is a written request or demand to an authority. The authority must examine it. A referendum, on the other hand, can only be signed by people entitled to vote.

key_terms.definition: District: administrative unit between canton and municipality; Zurich has 12 districts.
Petition: a written request to an authority that any person may submit.
Cantonal administration: the canton's offices that implement the laws; it is headed by the Cantonal Government.

zh_canton_tasks.mnemonic: 12 districts like the 12 months of the year.

municipal_politics.title: Municipal assembly, municipal council, City Council
intro: In the canton of Zurich there are 160 political municipalities (as of 2026). The learning brochures say «over 150». In the past there were more. Some municipalities have merged; this is called a municipal merger. The largest municipality is the city of Zurich; many others are small villages. In all municipalities, citizens have a say by taking part in elections and popular votes. The ballot papers are counted by the electoral office.

In most smaller municipalities there is no parliament. The voters meet at the municipal assembly (Gemeindeversammlung). There they decide directly, for example on the budget, taxes or large building projects. The government of such a municipality is called the municipal council (Gemeinderat). It is headed by the Municipal President (Gemeindepräsidentin or Gemeindepräsident). «Bürgermeister» (mayor) is the term used in Germany, not in the canton of Zurich.

Careful, a common mix-up: in the city of Zurich it is the other way round! There the government (executive) is called the City Council (Stadtrat). It has 9 members and runs the city administration. The parliament of the city of Zurich is called the Gemeinderat (City Parliament) and has 125 members. Both are elected by the people, every 4 years. In Winterthur the parliament is now called the Stadtparlament (City Parliament). The learning brochures still call it «Gemeinderat». In larger cities the top person is called the City President (Stadtpräsidentin or Stadtpräsident).

key_terms.definition: Municipal assembly: meeting of a municipality's voters that decides directly on the budget and important business.
City Council (city of Zurich): the government of the city of Zurich with 9 members.
City Parliament (city of Zurich): the parliament of the city of Zurich with 125 members.
Municipal President: the person who heads the municipal council of a smaller municipality and represents the municipality.
Electoral office: group of people who count the votes in elections and popular votes.

municipal_politics.mnemonic: In the CITY (Stadt) of Zurich, the STADTrat governs. There, the Gemeinderat is the parliament.

municipal_tasks.title: Tasks of the municipality
intro: The municipalities are the lowest of the three political levels. For people they are often the first point of contact. They carry out many tasks for which neither the Confederation nor the canton is responsible. Each municipality decides itself in its municipal code (Gemeindeordnung) how it is organised. The municipality is close to the people and knows the local situation.

Important tasks of the municipality are: organising kindergarten and primary school, water and waste water, waste, municipal roads and local spatial planning. Spatial planning means: the municipality decides where people may live, work or not build. That is why the municipality also grants the building permit, for example for a detached house.

The municipality runs the residents' registration office (Einwohnerkontrolle). All residents are registered there. Anyone who moves must deregister in the old municipality and register in the new municipality. Motorways, the military, foreign policy and monetary policy, on the other hand, are tasks of the Confederation. Universities of applied sciences are a matter for the canton.

key_terms.definition: Residents' registration office: municipal office where you register and deregister, for example when you move.
Building permit: permission from the municipality to build or convert a building.
Spatial planning: planning how land is used: where homes, companies or green spaces go.

municipal_tasks.mnemonic: Moving? Go to the municipality first!

zh_offices.title: Road Traffic Office and civil registry office
intro: In the canton of Zurich, the Road Traffic Office (Strassenverkehrsamt) is responsible for cars and driving. It belongs to the canton, not to the municipality. The Road Traffic Office holds driving tests and issues driving licences. It also inspects vehicles and registers them for use on the road. Then the car gets its number plates. The police, on the other hand, only check the traffic on the road. They do not issue driving licences and do not register cars. Car garages may not do this either.

Anyone who wants to get married goes to the municipality's civil registry office (Zivilstandsamt). The civil registry office keeps the civil status registers: birth, marriage, divorce and death. It checks whether the marriage is allowed and performs the wedding ceremony. Civil status is, for example, «single», «married» or «divorced».

key_terms.definition: Road Traffic Office: cantonal office for driving licences, driving tests and the registration of vehicles.
Civil registry office: office that registers birth, marriage and death and performs wedding ceremonies.
Civil status: a person's marital status, for example single or married.

zh_taxes.title: Cantonal and municipal taxes
intro: In Switzerland, the Confederation, the canton and the municipality levy taxes. The most important taxes for the canton and the municipality are income tax and wealth tax. You pay income tax on your wages and other income. You pay wealth tax on savings and property, for example a house.

In the canton of Zurich it is calculated like this: the municipality charges a percentage of the cantonal tax. This percentage is called the tax rate (Steuerfuss). It is different in each municipality. That is why you pay less tax in some municipalities than in others. But some taxes are collected only by the Confederation. These include withholding tax on interest, tobacco tax, alcohol tax and customs duties. So they are not part of the cantonal and municipal taxes.

key_terms.definition: Income tax: tax on wages and other income.
Wealth tax: tax on assets, for example savings or a house.
Tax rate: the percentage each municipality uses to calculate its tax; it differs from municipality to municipality.

zh_taxes.mnemonic: Canton and municipality tax what you earn and what you own.

zh_school.title: State schools in the canton of Zurich
intro: In Switzerland, the cantons and the municipalities are mainly responsible for state schools, not the Confederation. Compulsory school is called Volksschule. It is free of charge. The canton sets the rules and the curriculum. The municipalities organise and pay for the local schools, together with the canton.

In the canton of Zurich, compulsory schooling begins with kindergarten. Kindergarten lasts 2 years and is compulsory. Children who turn 4 by the end of July start kindergarten in August. After that come 6 years of primary school and 3 years of secondary school. So compulsory schooling lasts 11 years. Playgroup before kindergarten is voluntary.

Every school has a school management (Schulleitung). It runs the school day to day: it manages the teachers, organises lessons and is the contact for parents. The school board (Schulpflege) is the municipality's political authority that supervises the schools. The school secretariat helps with administration. At cantonal level, the Office for Compulsory Schooling (Volksschulamt) organises the schools and ensures the same rules.

key_terms.definition: State school: the compulsory public school: kindergarten, primary school and secondary school.
School management: the management of a school, which organises staff and lessons day to day.
Compulsory schooling: all children must attend school; in the canton of Zurich for 11 years, starting with kindergarten.

municipal_social.title: Social assistance, financial equalisation, neighbourhood association
intro: If someone can no longer live on their own income and assets, the municipality helps with social assistance. It covers the bare necessities: housing, food, health insurance. Social assistance is intended for emergencies and is paid for by the municipalities, with a contribution from the canton. The old-age pension (AHV), on the other hand, is an insurance of the Confederation.

Not all municipalities are equally rich. Some have many good taxpayers; others have little income or high social costs. Financial equalisation balances this out: rich municipalities and the canton pay money, poorer municipalities receive contributions.
