This way all municipalities can fulfil their tasks, for example schools and old people's homes.

A neighbourhood association (Quartierverein) represents the interests of the people in a part of the city vis-à-vis the authorities. It also organises festivals and meetings. Membership is voluntary. Information about the municipality's services and regulations can be found on the municipality's website and in the local newspaper, often in the official section.

key_terms.definition: Social assistance: financial help from the municipality for people who do not have enough money to live on.
Financial equalisation: system in which financially strong municipalities and the canton support poorer municipalities.
Neighbourhood association: voluntary association that stands up for the residents of a neighbourhood.

zh_location.title: Coat of arms, location and neighbouring cantons
intro: The canton of Zurich is in the north of Switzerland, in the Plateau (Mittelland). The Plateau is the flat to hilly area between the Jura and the Alps. Most people in Switzerland live here. On the map you find Zurich at the top in the middle, shifted a little to the right. In the north the canton borders on Germany; the border is partly formed by the Rhine.

Zurich borders on 6 cantons: in the north on Schaffhausen, in the east on Thurgau and St. Gallen, in the south on Schwyz and Zug, in the west on Aargau. Lucerne, Glarus and Fribourg are not neighbours of Zurich. In addition there is the border with Germany in the north. Lake Zurich is mostly in the canton of Zurich; a small part belongs to Schwyz and St. Gallen.

The coat of arms of the canton of Zurich is divided diagonally into white and blue. The line goes from top left to bottom right. The top right field is white, the bottom left is blue. There is no animal and no cross in the coat of arms. Other coats of arms look similar: Lucerne is divided vertically into blue and white, Zug is white with a blue horizontal bar, Ticino is vertically red and blue.

key_terms.definition: Plateau: the flat to hilly area between the Jura and the Alps, where most people live.
Coat of arms: the emblem of a canton or municipality; Zurich: divided diagonally into white and blue.

zh_location.mnemonic: Zurich coat of arms: white sky above, blue lake below, divided diagonally. Neighbours: «SH, TG, SG, SZ, ZG, AG» = 6.

zh_cities.title: Cities, airport, population
intro: More people live in the canton of Zurich than in any other canton. The learning brochures give 1.5 million (as of 2020). Since then the population has continued to grow: at the end of 2025 there were around 1.63 million. Almost one fifth of all people in Switzerland live here. Many people come to the city of Zurich every day to work.

The capital of the canton is the city of Zurich. It is also the largest city in Switzerland, with over 400'000 inhabitants. The second-largest city in the canton is Winterthur, with over 100'000 people. Uster comes third. Zug, Cham, Baden and Wettingen are not in the canton of Zurich.

Zurich Airport is the largest airport in Switzerland. It is not in the city of Zurich, but north of it in the municipality of Kloten. That is why it is sometimes also called «Kloten Airport». Kloten belongs to the district of Bülach. From the airport it takes around 10 minutes by train to Zurich main station.

key_terms.definition: Capital: the town where a canton's government and parliament have their seat; for Zurich this is the city of Zurich.

zh_cities.mnemonic: The three largest: Zurich, Winterthur, Uster: «ZWU».

zh_waters.title: Lakes, rivers and hills
intro: The largest lake in the canton is Lake Zurich. The second-largest is Lake Greifen, followed by Lake Pfäffikon. Both are in the Zurich Oberland, east of the city of Zurich. Lake Zug, Lake Hallwil, Lake Sempach, Lake Walen and Lake Sihl are in other cantons.

Lake Zurich is surrounded by three hills: in the west by the Uetliberg and the Albis, in the east by the Pfannenstiel. The Uetliberg is the city of Zurich's local mountain. The highest mountain in the canton is the Schnebelhorn in the Zurich Oberland. Other mountains are the Bachtel, the Hörnli and the Schauenberg. The Lägern is in the north, the Randen in the canton of Schaffhausen.

The Limmat flows out of Lake Zurich. It flows right through the city of Zurich and later into the canton of Aargau. In the city of Zurich the Sihl flows into the Limmat, at the Platzspitz behind the main station. The Töss flows through Winterthur. Other rivers are the Glatt, the Thur and the Rhine on the northern border. The Aare, the Rhone, the Inn and the Ticino do not flow through the canton of Zurich.

key_terms.definition: Limmat: river that flows out of Lake Zurich through the city of Zurich.
Sihl: river that flows into the Limmat in the city of Zurich.
Töss: river that flows through Winterthur.

zh_waters.mnemonic: Lakes by size: Lake Zurich, Lake Greifen, Lake Pfäffikon. «Z-G-P».

zh_land.title: Kyburg and agriculture
intro: The canton of Zurich is not only city. Around 41 percent of the area is used for agriculture, that is for fields, meadows and pastures. About 30 percent is forest, and almost a quarter is settlement area with houses, roads and factories. The rest is mainly lakes, rivers and wetlands. There are many farms above all in the Weinland in the north and in the Zurich Oberland.

The best-known castle in the canton is Kyburg. It stands on a hill above the Töss, near Winterthur. Kyburg is around 1000 years old and is a museum today. Other famous castles are in other cantons: Chillon in Vaud, Hallwyl in Aargau and Gruyères in Fribourg.

key_terms.definition: Agricultural area: land used for fields, meadows and pastures; in Zurich around 41 percent.
Kyburg: medieval castle near Winterthur, today a museum.

zh_ancient.title: Pile dwellings and Turicum
intro: People already lived on Lake Zurich more than 6000 years ago. From about 5000 to 1000 BC they built pile dwellings. These are houses on wooden posts, called piles, on the shores of lakes and rivers. This protected people from floods and animals. Remains of these houses still lie in the water today. They are part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

Later the Romans came. They called the place where the lake flows out Turicum. The name Zurich came from this. Among other things, the Romans brought bathing culture and their language. They built public baths (thermae). Remains of a Roman bath can be seen in Zurich's old town in the Thermengasse. Other Roman names belong to other places: Vitudurum is Winterthur, Vindonissa is Windisch, Aquae Helveticae is Baden.

key_terms.definition: Pile dwellings: houses on wooden piles on lake shores from the Stone Age and Bronze Age.
Turicum: the Roman name of Zurich.

zh_ancient.mnemonic: TuRIcum, ZüRIch, ZuRIgo: the Italian name Zurigo still recalls Turicum.

zh_reformation.title: Zwingli and the plague
intro: Ulrich (also Huldrych) Zwingli lived from 1484 to 1531. From 1519 he was a pastor at the Grossmünster in Zurich. He wanted to renew the church and base it only on the Bible. This renewal is called the Reformation. Zwingli is the reformer of Zurich. Martin Luther was the reformer in Germany, John Calvin in Geneva.

With the Reformation, much changed in Zurich: Mass was abolished, pictures were removed from the churches, monasteries were dissolved. Church services were now in German instead of Latin. Zwingli also fought against mercenary service, that is against Swiss men who fought in foreign wars for money. He died in 1531 in the Battle of Kappel.

In the 17th century the plague came to Zurich several times, above all in 1611, 1629 and 1635. The plague is a highly contagious disease. About 25 million people died of it in all of Europe. According to the learning brochure, half of Zurich's population died between 1611 and 1635. More recent historical research speaks of up to 40 percent.

key_terms.definition: Reformation: renewal of the church in the 16th century; the Reformed Church emerged from it.
Reformer: a person who led the Reformation, for example Zwingli in Zurich.
Plague: dangerous contagious disease that killed many people in the past.

zh_reformation.mnemonic: Zwingli = Zurich, Luther = Germany, Calvin = Geneva.

zh_modern.title: Canton since 1803, Lieberherr, chocolate
intro: Zurich has been part of the Confederation since 1351. Until 1798 Zurich was a city state: the city ruled over the countryside. In 1798 the French came, and the old order ended. In 1803 Napoleon gave Switzerland a new constitution (Act of Mediation). The canton of Zurich in the modern sense has existed since 1803. Now the people in the countryside could also help elect the cantonal parliament.

During the Second World War (1939 to 1945) there was less and less food in Switzerland. That is why potatoes and vegetables were planted everywhere, even on public squares in the cities. This was called the «Anbauschlacht» (cultivation battle). The Sechseläutenplatz in Zurich was also used as a potato field. Today it is a large square next to the opera house.

Emilie Lieberherr (1924 to 2011) was a famous campaigner for women's rights. She organised protests for women's suffrage throughout Switzerland. In 1969 she spoke at the «March on Bern». In 1971 the men said yes to women's suffrage. In 1970 she was elected as the first woman to the Zurich City Council, and later also to the Council of States.

Switzerland is known for chocolate. In the 19th century, pioneers founded the first large chocolate factories. Philippe Suchard founded a factory in Neuchâtel in 1826, Rudolph Lindt in Bern in 1879. Lindt invented a method that makes chocolate melt smoothly. The company Lindt & Sprüngli has its headquarters today in Kilchberg on Lake Zurich.

key_terms.definition: Act of Mediation: constitution that Napoleon gave Switzerland in 1803; since then the canton of Zurich has existed in its present form.
Women's suffrage: the right of women to vote and elect; at federal level since 1971.
Cultivation battle: plan in the Second World War to grow as much food as possible in Switzerland itself.

zh_sechselaeuten.title: Sechseläuten, Böögg and guilds
intro: Sechseläuten is the best-known spring festival in Zurich. It takes place in April, usually on the third Monday. In the past, on this day the bell rang at 6 p.m. for the first time as a sign of the end of the working day in summer. That is where the name comes from (Sechs = six, läuten = ring).

The guilds play an important role. Sechseläuten is a festival of the guilds. Guilds used to be associations of craftspeople, for example bakers or blacksmiths. They organised their trades and trained young people. In the city of Zurich they also used to have political power. Today they are traditional associations. At Sechseläuten they parade through the city in historical costumes.

At 6 p.m. the guilds set fire to the Böögg on the Sechseläutenplatz. The Böögg is a large figure made of wood and cotton wool that looks like a snowman. There are firecrackers in its head. It stands for winter. After it is lit, people wait until its head explodes. Tradition says: the faster the Böögg loses its head, the nicer the coming summer will be.

key_terms.definition: Sechseläuten: Zurich spring festival in April with a parade of the guilds.
Böögg: snowman figure that is burned at Sechseläuten and represents winter.
Guild: in the past an association of craftspeople, today a traditional association in Zurich.

zh_sechselaeuten.mnemonic: Böögg's head falls quickly = summer will be nice.

zh_events.title: Street Parade, Theater Spektakel, Weltklasse
intro: The Street Parade is a big techno festival in Zurich. It took place for the first time in 1992 and is also very well known abroad. Every summer hundreds of thousands of people dance around the lake basin. The Street Parade stands for love, peace, freedom, generosity and tolerance. Its music is electronic, not folk music.

The Zürcher Theater Spektakel takes place every year in August on the Landiwiese on Lake Zurich. Groups from all over the world show theatre, dance and music there. Another big festival is the Albanifest in Winterthur, with around 100'000 visitors. In many municipalities there is also a «Chilbi» with festival stalls and rides.

Weltklasse Zürich is a well-known athletics meeting at the Letzigrund stadium. The best athletes in the world compete there. Other sports events take place elsewhere: the Engadin Skimarathon in the canton of Graubünden, the Swiss Indoors (tennis) in Basel, the Schweizer Frauenlauf in Bern.

key_terms.definition: Street Parade: big techno festival in Zurich for love, peace, freedom, generosity and tolerance.
Weltklasse Zürich: international athletics meeting at the Letzigrund stadium.

zh_museums.title: Technorama, Masoala, Gottfried Keller
intro: The Technorama in Winterthur is a science centre. Here you may touch everything and experiment yourself, for example with light, magnets or water. In other museums you can usually only look at the exhibits, for example in the Reinhart Collection «Am Römerholz» or in the Fotomuseum, which are also in Winterthur.

In the city of Zurich there are many well-known museums, for example the Swiss National Museum, the Kunsthaus and the Museum Rietberg. Zurich Zoo is also very popular. It has the Masoala Hall. This is a large hall with a rainforest like on the island of Madagascar. Animals and plants from Madagascar live there, for example lemurs and chameleons.

Gottfried Keller (1819 to 1890) was a famous Zurich writer. He was also a painter and politician. His best-known book is the novel «Der grüne Heinrich» (Green Henry). He also wrote the stories «Die Leute von Seldwyla» (The People of Seldwyla). For many years he worked as State Secretary (Staatsschreiber) of the canton of Zurich. He is one of the most important Swiss authors of the 19th century.

key_terms.definition: Technorama: science centre in Winterthur where you can experiment yourself.
Masoala Hall: rainforest hall at Zurich Zoo with animals and plants from Madagascar.

guide.title: Grundkenntnistest Zurich: how the citizenship test works
guide.desc: Who has to take the Zurich naturalisation knowledge test, which questions come up, where it takes place and what it costs. Official sources only.
guide.lede: What the Canton and the City of Zurich officially say about the test, with sources.

a: For ordinary naturalisation in the Canton of Zurich you need knowledge of Switzerland, the Canton of Zurich and the municipalities of Zurich. You prove it in a test with questions about geography, politics and history.
The legal basis is § 16 of the cantonal citizenship ordinance (KBüV): the municipality checks basic knowledge either in a naturalisation interview with a standardised questionnaire or with a test.

faq.q: Do I have to take the test?
a: You do not have to take the test if one of these applies:

• You are younger than 12.
  • You currently attend compulsory school or upper secondary education (apprenticeship, Gymnasium) in Switzerland.
  • You attended compulsory school in Switzerland for 5 years, at least 3 of them at lower secondary level.
  • You completed upper secondary education in Switzerland.
The canton's self-check tells you for your situation. In the City of Zurich, people in the facilitated naturalisation procedure have their knowledge checked in the naturalisation interview.
The canton publishes the list of all 350 questions (PDF, German, May 2025). Each question has 4 answers, exactly one is correct.
The canton's official practice test asks 50 questions and shows after each answer whether it was correct. Whether the real test has the same format is not officially confirmed.

faq.q: Where and when is the test?
a: Your municipality tells you when and where you can take the test. Ask your municipality to register. Depending on the municipality, you take the test before or after you submit your application.
In the City of Zurich the test takes place in the Stadthaus, only after you have submitted your application.

faq.q: How much does the test cost?
a: Fees differ by municipality and test provider. Ask your municipality. In the City of Zurich the test is free.

faq.q: What is the pass mark? How long does the test take?
a: Neither is officially published, so we do not give numbers here. The canton's Gemeindeamt answers questions: grundkenntnistest@ji.zh.ch, +41 43 259 83 81 (Mon to Thu 13:30 to 17:00, Fri 13:30 to 16:00).
The canton offers the practice test, the naturalisation brochure and the list of all questions.

sections: Who

Swiss Passport is a free, non-commercial project by Aleksej Dix and Lidia Dix. We live in the Canton of Zurich and are preparing for our own naturalisation, so we built the tool we were missing. The code and the content are open on GitHub.

For more than ten years, Aleksej has co-organised the tech community WebZurich and helps organise conferences in Zurich. Every year Aleksej collects computers and gives them to families who need them for learning, mostly for the children. Lidia co-organises WebZurich too and helps organise events for women who are new in Zurich: theatre visits, excursions and workshops on how Switzerland works.

The 350 questions and their correct answers come from the official question list of the Canton of Zurich (Gemeindeamt, Abteilung Einbürgerungen, May 2025).

method.title: How to learn for the citizenship test: the method behind Swiss Passport
method.desc: Why answering questions and repeating them at growing intervals works better than rereading, and how Swiss Passport uses it to prepare you for the Zurich knowledge test.
method.lede: Most people prepare by reading the questions again and again. It feels productive, but it is one of the least effective ways to learn. Swiss Passport uses techniques that memory research has tested for decades.
sections: Answer instead of rereading

Every time you pull an answer out of your memory, you strengthen it. In a well-known study, students who practised recalling a text remembered more of it a week later than students who read it again, even though rereading did better right after studying (Roediger & Karpicke 2006).
That is why Swiss Passport shows a short explanation and then asks right away. You answer every question yourself before you see the solution.
Repeat just before you forget

What you learn fades quickly if you do not use it again. Repetitions spread over days and weeks keep knowledge much longer than the same amount of practice in one go. The longer you need to remember something, the longer the gaps can be (Cepeda et al. 2006).

Swiss Passport brings every topic back after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days. If you answer correctly, the next gap gets longer. If you make a mistake, the topic moves back one step and comes back the next day. So you practise what you forget and skip what you know.
Learn from every answer

After each answer you see why it is right, and if you chose a wrong one, why that tempting option is wrong. This matters especially for multiple-choice questions: without feedback, learners sometimes later take a wrong option for true; with feedback, this effect gets smaller (Butler & Roediger 2008).
A question you get wrong comes back at the end of the lesson until you answer it correctly.
Mix topics before the test

In the real test the questions come in no particular order. Reviews mix topics from different lessons, and every mock exam asks 50 random questions from all 350, without help, like the canton's practice test. Mixed practice feels harder, but in studies it led to better results on later tests than practising one topic at a time (Rohrer & Taylor 2007).
Your readiness score shows the share of questions whose topic you have already answered correctly on several days.
Understand in your language, recognise the German

You learn in the language you understand best, so you understand the content instead of memorising words. Every question also shows the German wording used in the real test, so you recognise it there.
Why this matters for your test
There are 350 official questions, and your municipality tells you when you take the test. Cramming the evening before may help the next day, but what you cram fades quickly.
A large review of learning techniques rates practice testing and spaced practice as the two most useful, and rereading and highlighting as of low use (Dunlosky et al. 2013).
In short: a little every day beats a lot at once. Do one short lesson a day, and the due reviews first.

built_text: Each lesson covers one to five topics. Every topic has a short explanation and the official questions that go with it.

order_text: You can start the lessons of stage 1 right away. The others build on the lessons listed with them: to learn about federalism, you should already know what a democracy is.
